#3523. We Officially Ranked Every Alien Movie

The Alien franchise is one of the most totemic in sci-fi and horror cinema. A lot of that legacy comes from the first two installments, which are universally considered great and have inspired a lot of spirited debate over which is superior. Beyond those films, the additional seven that feature xenomorphs have experienced varying degrees of appreciation over the years. Outside the variations in tone, that appreciation usually comes down to the difference between intent and execution.

There have been Alien movies that attempt ambitious expansions of the franchise by going well off course and there have been technically well-made movies that stay safely on the established rails. Individual appreciation of those films can really come down to the singular preferences of each fan. All that debate and personal differences can be put to bed now that we’ve officially ranked every Alien movie.

A movie that even the most die hard fans of either franchise would have trouble defending, Aliens vs. Predator: Requiem fails in almost every respect. It’s a bad Alien movie, it’s a bad Predator movie, and it’s bad at being a movie. The film’s notoriously poor lighting and editing make many scenes near incomprehensible, not that being able to see or understand what’s going on would make the movie much better.

Picking up directly after Alien vs. Predator, the movie at least makes good on its predecessor's promise of the Predalien hybrid monster, which crash lands back on Earth and begins wreaking havoc on a small town in Colorado. Space truckers, scientists, and Colonial Marines are replaced here with stock characters more suited to a slasher, which is really what this movie is, just dressed up in the hollowed out corpses of both beloved franchises. The only element worth applauding in the movie is the effects work, which should come as no surprise as directors Greg and Colin Strause have a background in visual effects. Even then, the creature effects, by Amalgamated Dynamics, are hidden in almost complete darkness. The abject failure of this film is what led both franchises to split back apart to try and find their own identities again.

Alien: Resurrection is not a good movie, by any measure, but it is a weird movie, and that counts for something. It was ill-advised to bring the character of Ripley back after her demise in Alien 3, even if she is a completely different clone character here. Sigourney Weaver, at the very least, gets to explore some strange territory with this iteration, and director Jean-Pierre Jeunet is more than happy to make things bizarre and sexual. The visuals are striking, the practical effects, again by Amalgamated Dynamics, are impressive and Alien: Resurrection is straight up one of the oddest blockbusters ever made.

In the film, Ripley has somehow been cloned in the even more distant future, along with a xenomorph embryo inside her. After some mad space scientists do their thing, the aliens escape and all hell breaks loose. Ripley has to team up with a motley crew of space pirates who were a clear progenitor for writer Joss Whedon’s later work on Firefly. The Whedon banter is discordant with Jeunet’s directorial style and the performances, which adds to the overall strange tone of this grotesque movie. Alien: Resurrection was the final nail in the space coffin for the franchise’s original continuity, but it’s got a weird charm for those in the right mood for it.

There is nothing artistic or narratively interesting about Alien vs. Predator. It’s a movie made purely for financial reasons and fan service. It doesn’t attempt to elevate the genre in any way and is more than happy to just be a B movie. There’s nothing wrong with that and there are a few moments in the movie that are enjoyable on a brainless blockbuster level. Unfortunately, those moments are spread thin across an overwritten story with underwritten characters and a PG-13 rating that doesn’t provide enough of the carnage that fans would expect from the first meeting of these two sci-fi monster titans.

Paul W.S. Anderson makes sense on paper for a film like this. He’s a steady hand at making slick genre movies that turn a tidy profit, but AVP shares more in common with his braindead Resident Evil movies than his more visceral Event Horizon. It follows a group of interchangeable experts and mercenaries who venture into an underground pyramid in Antarctica that was used by the Predators for ceremonial hunts using alien prey. The plot threads itself into knots and leaves holes big enough to fit an oblong xenomorph head through, but it occasionally can get exciting when the movie stops to let its monsters mash each other into pulp. As fan service cash grabs go, AVP could be a lot worse, but it could have been so much better too.

Ridley Scott is the only director to have made more than one film in the Alien franchise. It’s fitting, since he started everything with the original classic, but each subsequent film has been a diminished return. The nadir is Alien: Covenant, a tonally confused mess caught between being the movie Scott wanted to make and the movie he thought Alien fans wanted. It tries to serve too many masters and ends up satisfying none. All that said, it is still an Alien movie directed by Ridley Scott, so it has some incredible visuals and violence, and Michael Fassbender giving a dual performance worthy of a much better movie.

After the lukewarm response to Prometheus, this sequel was reconfigured to lean more heavily into the horror elements of the earlier Alien films while still attempting to keep the philosophical themes of its predecessor. The biggest casualty of that change was Noomi Rapace’s character Elizabeth Shaw, who is killed off-screen, while Fassbender’s android David is upgraded to an evil villain. Fassbender also plays the more user-friendly Walter, who’s part of the wholly new cast of colonists who land on the alien planet that was once home to the Engineers and proceed to make a series of increasingly stupid decisions. Every moment of Covenant that does something new or interesting is immediately followed by something inane. The entire third act is a hollow retread of the first film and a painful reminder of how far Scott and the franchise have drifted astray.

Speaking of retreads, Alien: Romulus was designed to be a back-to-basics reinvigoration of the franchise, though it does still have connective tissue to Scott’s divisive prequels. Fede Álvarez was brought in to inject fresh acid blood, and while the director does craft some suitably suspenseful sequences, the film as a whole plays like the greatest hits of the franchise rather than its own unique experience. It’s also awkwardly inserted into the continuity between Alien and Aliens, and far too often relies on fan service instead of trying to create its own iconic moments. It’s still a solid reminder of why the Alien franchise is so beloved, but it doesn’t do anything to truly justify its existence.

The human, and android, characters here are a group of colonists trying to get out from under the corporate thumb of Weyland-Yutani, the villainous conglomerate that has featured heavily in every film. They escape their mining planet and connect with a seemingly abandoned space station that turns out to have been a research vessel studying the original film’s xenomorph that was found floating in space and then revived. From there, Alien: Romulus becomes a remix of fan favorite moments throughout the franchise, some executed better than others. The worst offender is the character of Rook, an android identical to Ash from the first film created using CGI to resurrect deceased actor Ian Holm. He’s a soulless recreation that’s technically impressive, much like a lot of the film itself.

Here’s where the true dividing line of intent versus execution comes down for the Alien franchise. For all its faults, Alien: Romulus is an undeniable accomplishment in recreating the mood and atmosphere of the early Alien movies. Prometheus, on the other hand, tries to distinguish itself from the franchise as its own sci-fi story exploring the background of the Engineers instead of rinsing and repeating. It’s an admirable idea, and one that was compelling enough to bring back Ridley Scott, but its execution is far from flawless. It’s hard to rank based on intent, but the ambition of Prometheus ultimately makes it more interesting, even if it does come crashing down by the end.

The fundamental flaw in Prometheus is that it seeks to explain things that were more interesting when they were left unexplained. The Engineer that appeared in Alien, known then as the Space Jockey, suggested an entire backstory to the origin of the xenomorph that was far more fascinating than what Prometheus ultimately offers. Following a scientific expedition to a far off planet that explains the origins of humanity and their creators, the movie is dealing with heavy themes of existential and cosmic horror, but every further plot development lessens the impact. The characters also make irrational decisions for no reason other than to serve the plot, and the tenuous prequel connections to Alien are more confusing than anything else. Much like co-writer Damon Lindelof’s Lost, Prometheus had so much promise but failed to deliver.

Much like Prometheus, what makes Alien 3 so interesting isn’t so much the movie that was made, but the movie that could have been made. The tortured production history of the third film in the franchise is too long to recount here, but the fact that David Fincher, in his directorial debut, was able to deliver a semi-coherent movie is nothing short of a cinematic miracle. Fincher has long since disowned the movie due to his disagreements with 20th Century Fox, but it has gained a strong cult following since its original release, partially thanks to the so-called Assembly Cut that attempted to edit the film closer to Fincher’s original vision.

Both versions of the movie are still disjointed and suffer from serious pacing issues and inconsistent characters. They also both begin with the beloved characters of Newt and Hicks from Aliens being killed off, a decision many franchise fans still take major issue with. Setting that all aside, the film, which finds Ripley contending with another xenomorph, this one born from an animal on a prison planet, is a nihilistic and nasty sci-fi horror movie that’s atmospheric as hell. Through all its flaws, Alien 3 still has moments that are individually effective, and that sometimes showcase Fincher’s directorial skills that would become more pronounced in his later films where he had more creative control. Alien 3 is far from perfect, but its imperfections are better than some of the best moments of the later films in the franchise.

Trying to rank Alien and Aliens is an impossible task. Both films are vastly different from one another yet remain thematically connected, but it’s their differences that make them individually great. What James Cameron accomplished with Aliens is a masterclass in sequel making. It expands on the core plot elements established in the first film without betraying them while also shifting the genre elements closer to what Cameron excels at as a filmmaker. Aliens is bigger, if not necessarily better, than Alien, but that increased size is tied directly to the plot of the film and isn’t an act of arbitrary inflation. Aliens is a different starbeast than Alien, and how it ranks against it is more dependent on personal preference than it is on the individual achievement of either film.

Sigourney Weaver famously received an Academy Award nomination for her performance in Aliens, and it’s really in this sequel where the character became a genre icon. Where she was a practical and intelligent protagonist in the first film, she was very much a part of the larger ensemble and defined mostly by Weaver’s performance than character traits. In Aliens, the character is given more dimension through both the trauma she sustained in the first film, and a greater motivation as maternal protector over Carrie Henn’s Newt, the sole survivor of the colony built on the alien planet LV-426 where Riley returns with a group of colorful and overconfident Colonial Marines. Using post-Vietnam disillusionment as a basis, Cameron establishes a militarized plot to drop Ripley into, and crafts a massively entertaining action-sci-fi-horror hybrid blockbuster around her.

The original Alien is still the best. The franchise may have evolved and expanded far beyond its humble beginnings, but there’s a purity in the first film that should be admired. From Dan O’Bannon and Ronald Shusett's original script that pulled influence from classic sci-fi pulps and B movies and synthesized them into a lean horror movie. From the influence of producers David Giler and Walter Hill, who introduced a working class versus corporate interests conflict to the plot. From the iconic production and creature designs of artists like Ron Cobb and H.R. Giger. From the ensemble cast that eschewed typical horror archetypes. From Ridley Scott’s focused direction and a million other elements that went into the film’s production, a sci-fi horror masterpiece burst forth and it hasn’t been improved upon since.

What began as Starbeast, a simple sci-fi concept destined to be a cheap Roger Corman production about astronauts who discover an alien lifeform on a strange planet and unwittingly bring one on board their ship, became one of the most influential sci-fi films of all time. It launched huge careers, was endlessly imitated and ripped off, including by Corman, and became permanently implanted in pop culture. Thousands of things had to go right, and wrong, for Alien to become the film it is. Thank the stars it did, because it’s hard to imagine what sci-fi, or horror, would like without, and how different both genres might be without the continued work of so many of those involved. It started the franchise that we all love and continue to debate to this day, and it’s still the best part of it, officially.

#3521. Apple earnings suggest the iPhone 18 launch strategy is really working

Yesterday’s AAPL earnings report revealed record revenue for a September quarter, and within it was an arguably even more significant record: iPhone revenue.

That’s because this year’s quarter only includes just two new iPhone models compared to the four released last year …

Apple reported fiscal quarter four revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year on year. Within that was iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion, which was also a quarterly record. What makes this significant is the year-on-year comparison, when you consider the new iPhone launch revenue included within each quarter.

(Although the iPhone Duo was announced at the same time, pre-orders didn’t open until October, so none of this revenue is included in Apple’s fiscal Q4.)

The main thing that changed this year is that Apple didn’t launch a base model iPhone 18 alongside the Pro models: that launch won’t happen until early next year. The biggest factor in this decision was likely component shortages, Apple wanting to ensure that it could fulfill demand for premium models, but the revenue figures suggest that the timings also influenced purchase decisions.

Many people upgrade their iPhones on a fixed cycle, be that every one, two, or three years – and that cycle begins each September. When upgrade time rolled around and there was no base model iPhone 18 available, it seems likely that a significant number of those who would have bought it decided to instead opt for the iPhone 18 Pro rather than wait.

That may suggest rather modest sales of the base model iPhone 18 when it rolls around, but if Apple managed to persuade a significant number of would-be buyers to opt for a more expensive model, the company won’t be shedding any tears about that.

Of course, there are a couple of other factors in the mix here. First, the iPhone 17 proved extremely popular and remains on sale today, so it will have contributed something to this year’s Q4 revenue. Second, Apple cited revenue rather than profit, and the $100 price increase for this year’s Pro models will played a role. But overall I do think it paints a very encouraging picture for this split launch strategy.

What’s your take? Do you think it reflects well on iPhone 18 Pro sales, or do you think it can be explained away by the price increase and continuing popularity of the iPhone 17? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …

Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.

Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect?

Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.

In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Unlike a traditional sequel, Heat 2 will explore the events both before and after the original movie. The movie will feature several other major actors, such as Leonardo DiCaprio, Stephen Graham, and Bale. Jerry Bruckheimer and Scott Stuber will serve as producers for the upcoming sequel.

#3514. New iPad mini hands-on: Refreshed design, OLED display, more

Apple’s smallest iPad has gotten its biggest update in years. The new iPad mini features a much thinner and lighter design, a larger OLED display, water resistance, and the powerful A20 Pro chip.

I’ve been testing the new iPad mini, and there’s a lot to like — but also a couple of frustrations. Here’s everything you need to know.

The new iPad mini lives up to the “mini” name even more than its predecessor. It’s significantly thinner, down from 6.3mm on the previous iPad mini to 5.4mm on the new model. In fact, that puts it very close to the ultra-thin iPad Pro and the unfolded iPhone Duo. Here’s how it compares:

The new iPad mini is also significantly lighter, dropping from 293 grams to 255 grams. That puts it in the realm of the iPhone Duo, for comparison’s sake:

The reduction in weight and thickness was immediately noticeable when I picked up the new iPad mini. It feels significantly nicer to hold, more premium, and less “dense” in my hands.

The new iPad mini features an 8.5-inch screen, a slight increase from the previous generation’s 8.3-inch display. The overall footprint is mostly the same (the new model is actually about 2.2mm narrower). The larger screen is possible because the new iPad mini’s bezels are 24 percent thinner than before.

In addition to allowing a bigger screen in the same form factor, the narrower bezels also modernize the iPad mini’s overall look and feel. The bezels are noticeably slimmer than the iPad Air and base model iPad, and slightly thinner than the iPad Pro.

With smaller bezels, a thinner chassis, and a lighter weight, the new iPad mini feels significantly more premium than before. It reminds me less of the base model iPad or iPad Air and more of the iPad Pro, just shrunken down.

The big news about the display, though, is the switch to OLED. This marks Apple’s first non-Pro iPad to offer an OLED screen. It’s not the fancy tandem OLED display of the iPad Pro, but it’s a huge improvement over the previous model’s LCD panel.

The new iPad mini offers SDR brightness up to 600 nits, up from the previous model’s 500 nits max. The iPad mini also supports HDR content, with up to 1200 nits peak brightness.

The new iPad mini’s screen is undeniably an improvement over its predecessor. All of the inherent benefits of OLED apply here, including better colors, improved contrast, higher brightness, and more.

Unfortunately, the new iPad mini’s screen has one limitation: it doesn’t support ProMotion, or a 120Hz refresh rate of any kind. Instead, it’s still locked to 60Hz. This is an incredibly frustrating decision that I can’t quite wrap my head around.

Apple touts the iPad mini’s OLED screen as offering significantly faster pixel response time than the previous generation’s LCD panel, leading to improvements like smoother scrolling and reduced motion blur.

I’ve noticed that things like swiping between Home Screen pages, scrolling social media, and system animations are noticeably smoother. They aren’t, however, as smooth as an Apple device with a ProMotion display, and they’re not a substitute for a higher refresh-rate display.

I’m sure Apple knows the iPad mini’s market, and it seems to have decided not to prioritize ProMotion based on that information. However, as someone who has longed for a so-called “iPad mini Pro” for years, I’m disappointed by the decision. The new iPad mini’s screen is so much better … I just wish Apple had gone that extra step and added ProMotion. We’ve reached a point where ProMotion should be table stakes, especially after Apple brought it to the base iPhone 17 last year.

For an extra $100, you can upgrade the new iPad mini to have a nano-texture display (on the 256GB and 512GB models).

I’m a huge fan of Apple’s nano-texture display and have it on my 14-inch MacBook Pro. On the iPad mini, I think it makes even more sense.

The iPad mini is ultra-portable, and you naturally carry it around and use it in different lighting environments. The nano-texture glass helps reduce reflections and glare in a wide variety of lighting conditions. I also really like the combination of the iPad mini’s book-like size and the nano-texture finish.

There is a slight tradeoff in color vibrancy compared to a glossy OLED screen, as on other Apple devices with nano-texture, but it’s a very minor difference in my experience. The screen still looks fantastic.

One of the more interesting changes with the new iPad mini is something Apple calls the “Acoustic Display.” Instead of traditional speakers with visible grilles, Apple has developed a new system that uses the display itself to produce sound.

Essentially, Apple has designed special woofers that vibrate the display to produce low and midrange frequencies. For higher frequencies, custom tweeters are hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure. Apple says this new system delivers louder audio, “punchier” bass, and clearer highs, despite the iPad mini’s significantly thinner design.

In practice, I think the new iPad mini sounds great. I’d choose headphones or an external speaker for serious music or video consumption, but day-to-day the iPad mini’s built-in speakers are perfectly adequate. (I’d bet that this Acoustic Display technology shows up in future iPhones too, and the iPad mini is serving as a test bed of sorts.)

The Acoustic Display also plays an important role in another major upgrade: water and dust resistance. The new iPad mini is IP67 rated, which means it can be immersed in 1 meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes. It’s the first iPad to have an official water-resistance rating.

Adding water resistance to the iPad mini is particularly notable given its size and portability. I naturally find myself wanting to take it everywhere, and water resistance makes that more feasible.

One use case where all these improvements really come together is reading. The thinner and lighter design, nano-texture glass, and water resistance make the new iPad mini the most compelling iPad yet to serve as an e-reader.

The new iPad mini is powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip, which I already covered in detail in my iPhone 18 Pro review. The short version: the A20 Pro chip gives you plenty of power for anything you can throw at the iPad mini today.

One detail worth calling out is that Apple uses two different versions of the A20 Pro in the iPad mini. The 128GB and 256GB models feature a five-core CPU and 16-core Neural Engine, while the 512GB model gets a six-core CPU and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. All three configurations feature the same seven-core GPU.

I don’t think anyone should buy the 512GB version of the iPad mini just for those extra cores. You should pick your iPad mini configuration based on how much storage you need, not the version of the A20 Pro chip. You don’t need to worry about performance with the new iPad mini. And perhaps most importantly, the A20 Pro chip ensures the iPad mini has enough headroom for the future.

There’s been a lot of consternation about where the iPad mini fits in a world where the iPhone Duo also now exists. It’s a fair question. After all, when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, the two devices share a similar form factor … but that’s really where the similarities end.

The iPad mini offers the full-fledged, unapologetic iPadOS experience. It supports the full multitasking prowess of an iPad Pro, including windowing and the menu bar. The new iPad mini also supports extended display mode, so you can plug it into an external display and extend your iPad experience there.

The iPad mini also gets iPadOS app layouts, and most importantly, a desktop-class browsing experience in Safari. It’s a remarkably capable device in a remarkably compact form factor. It fits where other iPads can’t, yet it runs the same version of iPadOS as other iPads.

The new iPad mini does all of that, but better than before. The thinner, lighter design paired with smaller bezels gives the new iPad mini a meaningful visual refresh. The added water resistance means you can do even more with the compact and pocketable iPad mini design.

But all of this comes at a higher price of $699. This marks the second price increase for the iPad mini this year. It started the year at $499, rose to $599 as part of Apple’s broader price increases in June, and is now $699 as of this refresh.

The new iPad mini also still starts with 128GB of storage. Increasing the base storage to 256GB would’ve helped ease some of the pain of that price increase. It’s also getting increasingly hard to manage a device with 128GB, particularly with the storage needs of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. The lack of ProMotion and Face ID also make the price increase sting more.

Ultimately, the iPad mini form factor is a joy to use. The design feels great in the hand, and having the full iPadOS experience in such a compact device remains impressive. It’s not quite the “iPad mini Pro” I’ve always wanted, but it’s big upgrade to a form factor that I’ve always loved.

#3513. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

#3512. Cannes 2026 Movies Sold: Kino Lorber Buys Clio Barnard’s BIFA Contender ‘I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning’

Last year’s Cannes Film Festival saw Neon acquire its eventual Palme D’Or winner “It Was Just an Accident” and make splashes with “The Secret Agent” and “Sirât,” while Netflix bought “Nouvelle Vague” and “Left-Handed Girl.” But we also saw some titles like MUBI’s “Die, My Love” and “Sound of Falling” that didn’t make the same splash when they arrived stateside, despite big critical buzz out of the festival.

Neon came into Cannes with a glut of titles, and there weren’t many American films, but that didn’t slow the market. We’ll be tracking every sale as it happens.

Buyer: Kino LorberSection: Directors’ FortnightDirector: Clio BarnardBuzz: Kino Lorber has quietly been building up its slate with curated, compelling Cannes picks. Their latest: Clio Barnard’s Audience Award winner, based on Keiran Goddard’s novel of the same name. The film is packed with rising names, includig Anthony Boyle, Joe Cole, Jay Lycurgo, Daryl McCormack, and Lola Petticrew, and follows five friends as they contend with the unexpected realities of modern living, set against the UK housing crisis. Related Stories I Remember ‘Rocky’: My Front Row Seat to the Marketing of a Million-to-One Blockbuster MUBI Has Cleared the Path for Sandra Hüller to Land Multiple Oscar Nominations This Season

The film was adapted by Irish playwright and screenwriter Enda Walsh. It has continued to screen on the international festival circuit, most recently at BFI London Film Festival, AFI Fest, and Rome Film Festival. It was also recently nominated for eight British Independent Film Awards, including best British independent film, best director, best screenplay, and best ensemble performance. Kino Lorber is planning a 2027 theatrical release followed by a digital, educational, and home video release.

Buyer: Sumerian PicturesSection: Directors’ FortnightDirector: Eivind LandsvikBuzz: Sumerian Pictures before it was a film distributor is a long time record label, and the still upstart film side has finally picked up a feature that has some music ties. “Low Expectations” is a Norwegian film that stars Marie Ulven, better known as the Norwegian indie bedroom singer girl in red. She stars in the film alongside “The Worst Person in the World” actor Anders Danielsen Lie as arguably a version of herself, a rising pop star whose growing success becomes harder to reconcile with her inner life, leading her to take a part-time job at a high school from her hometown. “Low Expectations” is Landsvik’s feature directorial debut after directing two shorts, one that was accepted into Cannes in 2023 called “Tits,” and another that won a Norwegian Film Critics prize, “Sofia, Last Summer” from 2021. The film actually opens this week, September 11 in Norway, but Sumerian will release it in North America in 2027.

Buyer: Independent Film Company and Sapan StudioSection: Out of CompetitionDirector: Leah NelsonBuzz: This hand-drawn animated black and white film has a stacked voice cast featuring Abbi Jacobson, Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Bryan Cranston, Beanie Feldstein, Seth Rogen, and Samira Wiley, as well as Pamela Adlon, Sarah Silverman, Bowen Yang, Wanda Sykes, Phil Rosenthal, Adam Shapiro, Pat Finn, and Sugar Lyn Beard. It’s adapted from a memoir/graphic novel and is a story about a mother and daughter struggling with an Alzheimer’s diagnosis. The film will first play in the Centrepiece section at TIFF, then the distributors will plan an awards season rollout late this year before opening wider in early 2027.

Buyer: KimStimSection: Un Certain RegardDirector: Katharina RivillisBuzz: Wim Wenders produced this debut film about a German exchange student living in New Mexico shortly after the 9/11 attacks on the U.S. and how the teenager begins to feel homesickness while abroad in the desert heat. KimStim is an upstart indie distributor, and it is planning a North American theatrical release in 2027.

Buyer: Zeitgeist Films in association with Kino LorberSection: Un Certain RegardDirector: Judith GodrècheBuzz: Based on a memoir by a Nobel Prize-winning author Annie Ernaux, “A Girl’s Story” follows Ernaux in 2020 on a book tour and then all the way back to her teen years in the summer of 1958 and is a reflection on the “cruelty of other girls and the bitterness of sexual initiation,” per the film’s synopsis. Our positive review called it a very faithful and loyal adaptation of the Nobel Laureate’s work and a strong entry among other recent Ernaux adaptations like “Happening” and “Simple Passion.” Godrèche, who was a figurehead in the French #MeToo movement, also directs her own daughter Tess Barthélemy in the lead role as the young Ernaux. Zeitgeist is planning a release at New York’s Film Forum in April 2027 followed by a national rollout.

Buyer: Kino LorberSection: CompetitionDirector: Rodrigo SorogoyenBuzz: Per IndieWire’s review by Ryan Lattanzio — Javier Bardem plays a hotheaded filmmaker, one of those “brilliant assholes” mostly incapable of making great art without wringing it out of tyrannical behavior, in Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s Spanish industry drama “The Beloved.” The director of a memorable 2019 movie called “Madre,” a warped tale of motherhood in which a woman strikes up an affair with a dead ringer of her long-lost son, now turns his camera (or cameras, as Sorogoyen experiments with many visual formats to bewildering effect here) on fatherhood and its sins. Bardem stars as Esteban Martinez, who is casting the leading female role in his new film “Desierto,” a role he has written for his estranged daughter Emilia (Victoria Luengo).

Kino Lorber plans a qualifying run in 2026 with an awards push for Bardem, then a broader North American release in 2027. Deadline first reported the news.

Buyer: Watermelon PicturesSection: Special ScreeningsDirector: Diego LunaBuzz: The “Andor” star directed this immigrant drama film about a young woman who relocates from Mexico to Spain in order to reconnect with her mother. Star Anna Díaz earned praise for her performance, and she holds her own alongside her mother played by Adriana Paz. The film next plays TIFF, and no release plans have been set. Read more here.

Buyer: Greenwich EntertainmentSection: CompetitionDirector: Kōji FukadaBuzz: This Japanese drama follows an artist and an architect each grappling with the remnants of past relationships who connect in the rural Nagi region of Japan. Greenwich is planning a theatrical release in the U.S. and Canada in early 2027.

Buyer: Sony Pictures ClassicsSection: Out of CompetitionDirector: Andy GarciaBuzz: A true labor of love, star Andy Garcia also wrote, directed, and produced this throwback detective noir (he also designed all the music and co-wrote the original score with his longtime collaborator Arturo Sandoval), which he’s been working on for nearly 20 years.

In the film, Garcia stars as Joe Diamond, billed by SPC as “a man out of time, an urban legend with an emotional traumatic past. He has the uncanny ability to solve crimes that even the LAPD cannot — armed only with the savvy and dry humor reminiscent of the gumshoe detectives of that genre. It is a love letter to Los Angeles and an homage to the great noir films of the past.”

The film also stars Vicky Krieps, Brendan Fraser, Bill Murray, Dustin Hoffman, Rosemarie DeWitt, and more. Sony Pictures Classics acquired worldwide rights (ex. France, Germany, Italy, CIS) to the film and will announce release plans at a later date.

Buyer: Kino LorberSection: Director’s FortnightDirector: Reed Van DykBuzz: The directorial debut of Reed Van Dyk was a stunner out of Director’s Fortnight, with our critic writing that it is an “intimate and psychologically astute” war film based on a 2012 New Yorker article about the aftermath of the Iraq War and the impact of U.S. influence in the region. The film follows a U.S. Marine who returns to Iraq to visit with an Iraqi woman and her family whom were caught up in a firefight when he was deployed. The film stars Boyd Holbrook, Kenneth Branagh, and Hiam Abbass. Kino Lorber is planning a fall release with some awards ambitions in mind, and it will play some other fall festivals before then.

Buyer: 1-2 SpecialSection: CompetitionDirector: Emmanuel MarreBuzz: 1-2 Special’s third acquisition out of Cannes is writer/director Emmanuel Marre’s (“Zero Fucks Given”) historical drama “A Man of His Time,” starring Swann Arlaud, best known for his role in 2023’s Palme d’Or winner “Anatomy of a Fall.” Set in 1940, it’s inspired by the life of the filmmaker’s own great-grandfather, with Arlaud’s Henri arriving in Vichy, France, as Nazis began to install themselves. There, he ingratiates himself with the regime against the backdrop of French resistance. Per the distributor, “As he sets his plan into motion, he does whatever is required to remain useful, serving the machinery of the new order with increasing skill, but as the war continues he may be pursuing something more urgent: escape from his own ruin.” Winner of the Best Screenplay prize out of the Cannes competition, “A Man of His Time” will open in theaters next year.

Buyer: Kino LorberSection: Un Certain RegardDirector: Manuela MartelliBuzz: Kino Lorber’s first acquisition from Cannes is this Chilean film from the director of the Pinochet-era political thriller “Chile ’76.” This one though is set in 1992 after the end of the Pinochet regime and follows a young girl at a ski resort who befriends a German competitive skier, only for the German to disappear without a trace. Our critic compared the eerie mystery to “Picnic at Hanging Rock” and “The Spirit of the Beehive.” Kino Lorber picked up U.S. rights and is planning a theatrical release for early 2027.

Buyer: 1-2 SpecialSection: Un Certain RegardDirector: Sandra WollnerBuzz: Rising outfit 1-2 Special’s mandate at this year’s Cannes? It seems like “get proven winners.” After previously picking up Critics’ Week winner “La Gradiva,” the label has next bought Un Certain Regard winner “Everytime” the third film from filmmaker Sandra Wollner. The features tracks a family as they take a trip to the Canary Islands after a horrible tragedy.

Buyer: Janus FilmsSection: CompetitionDirector: Valeska GrisebachBuzz: “Western” filmmaker Grisebach’s Cannes contender, starring Yana Radeva and Syuleyman Letifov, premiered in the Competition section at the festival, where it was ultimately awarded the Jury Prize. The dreamy drama also sparkles with other genre beats, and our critic hailed its inventive spin on the Western, also noting that “Grisebach has a flair for finding faces with striking, weatherbeaten features that might have grown out of the landscape itself. We are in an era where the cinema normalizes faces interrupted by Botox and fillers, amounting to propaganda against aging and even mortality itself; by contrast, the faces that fill Grisebach’s frames are a cool drink of mountain water.” Janus Films will announce theatrical release plans in the coming weeks.

Buyer: NetflixSection: CompetitionDirector: Marie KreutzerBuzz: “Corsage” director Marie Kreutzer’s latest feature “Gentle Monster,” one of two competition films led by French star Léa Seydoux, marked Netflix’s third Cannes acquisition after the animated “In Waves” and Spanish epic “The Black Ball.” (Deadline first reported the news; IndieWire independently confirmed it.) The streamer obviously sees awards prospects in all three films, with Seydoux as a possible Best Actress contender for her performance as an avant-garde pianist whose life is blown apart by the news that her husband may be a child sex offender. Of the two Léa Seydoux films, “Gentle Monster” stood out over Neon’s “The Unknown” in terms of review response.

Buyer: MubiSection: CompetitionDirector: Lukas DhontBuzz: Mubi, which came to Cannes with “Minotaur” and “Fatherland” already in competition, just made its first acquisition for North America since the start of the festival with Lukas Dhont’s “Coward.” The Belgian filmmaker was nominated for the Best International Feature Oscar in 2023 for “Close”; here, he directs the furtive romance between two soldiers on the Western front in World War I. The film stars Emmanuel Macchia in his debut film performance as Pierre and Valentin Campagne (“Colours of Time,” “Case 137”) as Francis. Mubi already had rights in UK, Ireland, Germany, Austria, Italy, Spain, Turkey, Latin America, Australia, and New Zealand. The Match Factory, which has been part of Mubi since 2022, handles international sales.

Buyer: NetflixSection: CompetitionDirector: Javier Calvo and Javier AmbrossiBuzz: Rising filmmakers (and exes!) Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi premiered “The Black Ball” late in the competition to strong reviews and enthusiastic audience response. As Variety reported, a multi-studio bidding war ensued, with Mubi, A24, and Netflix, who eventually won out, in the mix. Set in 1932, 1937, and 2017 and following the lives of three men, the film is a tribute to poet Federico García Lorca and his unfinished works.

Buyer: Sony Pictures ClassicsSection: Special ScreeningsDirector: Pegah AhangaraniBuzz: Winner of the L’Oeil d’Or, this debut feature documentary from Iranian filmmaker Pegah Ahangarani is a deeply personal and autobiographical portrait of her own family that stretches 40 years, dating back to 1979 and up through the war going on in Iran as we speak. SPC, after grabbing “Iron Boy” earlier this week, landed all rights for North and Latin America, Asia (except Japan), New Zealand, Turkey, Portugal, and worldwide airlines.

Buyer: 1-2 SpecialSection: Critics’ WeekDirector: Marine AtlanBuzz: Our critic was enamored with the directorial debut of Marine Atlan, writing that it takes the simple premise of high school teens on a class trip and resists all tropes to find a film that nears “the sublime” and manages to “explore the vast worlds of their individual interiority with insight, empathy, and grace.” Just today the film won the Grand Prize from Critics’ Week, and it’s already one of the top 5 rated films on Letterboxd among this year’s crop of Cannes titles. 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release.

Buyer: Sony Pictures ClassicsSection: Un Certain RegardDirector: Louis ClichyBuzz: Yet another animated sale among the Official Selection, “Iron Boy” is a hand-painted animated feature with director Clichy, who cut his teeth as a 3D animator on “WALL-E” and “Up,” returning to ink line drawings inspired by Manga comics and his own early short films. “Iron Boy” is his first feature as a solo director. The film follows 11-year-old in rural France as he tries to live up to his rigid and distant father on the family farm. But when the young boy starts to lean over and collapse without warning, he must wear an iron corset to keep himself upright. Clichy co-wrote the film with Franck Salomé.

Buyer: NetflixSection: Critics WeekDirector: Phuong Mai NguyenBuzz: The opening night film for the Critics Week sidebar, Netflix acquired the worldwide rights (excluding France) for this animated film that features the voice talent of Will Sharpe and Stephanie Hsu. The film is based on a graphic novel by AJ Dungo and follows a shy teenager in Los Angeles who falls madly in love with a surfer girl, only for their love and future to be tested when she faces a sudden illness, leaning on their new passion for surfing and the ocean to get them through adversity. Fanny Burdino and Samuel Doux. Read our review here.

Buyer: A24Section: Un Certain RegardDirector: Jordan FirstmanBuzz: Arguably the smash hit of the Cannes Film Festival, comedian/actor Jordan Firstman writes, directs, and stars in this New York comedy as a washed-up party promoter who wakes up one day to find the child he never knew he had on his doorstep. The cast includes Cara Delevigne, Diego Calva, and newcomer Reggie Absolom, with producers including Oscar-winning “Anora” producer Alex Coco. and Galen Core, alongside Topic Studios’ Ryan Heller and Michael Bloom. A24 acquired the film’s rights in a competitive situation, with most major distributors bidding at Cannes. Read our review here.

Buyer: Clockwork (Warner Bros.)Section: Cannes ClassicsDirector: Ken RussellBuzz: This uncut restoration of Ken Russell’s super controversial — and largely unavailable — gem “The Devils” is being positioned by Warner Bros.’ new indie label Clockwork as the experience Russell always envisioned but never got to show properly. It’s the first repertory release from the new WB label, and frankly the first release period after announcing that Sean Baker’s next film “Ti Amo” was its inaugural acquisition. After it premieres in Cannes Classics, Clockwork is planning a one-week special engagement of screenings in theaters beginning October 16. Read more about the re-release here.

Buyer: NeonSection: CompetitionDirector: James GrayBuzz: “Paper Tiger” is the sixth film James Gray has brought to Cannes, but it’s the first time Neon has partnered with him, and given that it’s one of just two American films in the competition slate this year and one of the starriest, it seems like a match made in heaven. Gray’s crime thriller stars Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson, and Miles Teller in a story about two brothers striving to achieve the American Dream only to get caught up with the Russian Mafia.

Buyer: Janus FilmsSection: Cannes PremieresDirector: Kiyoshi KurosawaBuzz: The latest film from the director of “Cloud” is a samurai film set in 16th century Japan that follows a Lord who rebelled against a tyrannical ruler and found himself beseiged within his own castle by a traitor and a prisoner being held in his own dungeon. Though based on real individuals, the film is an original story by Honobu Yonezawa.

Section: CompetitionDistributor: MUBIDirector: Andrey ZvyagintsevBuzz: The first film from the Russian director behind “Leviathan” and “Loveless” in almost a decade is a political fable and crime thriller about a businessman caught up in personal, political, and professional scandals.

Title: “All of a Sudden” Section: CompetitionDistributor: NeonDirector: Ryusuke HamaguchiBuzz: After winning at Venice with “Drive My Car” and at Berlin with “Evil Does Not Exist,” the Japanese auteur is looking for the European festival trifecta with Neon backing his Palme D’Or bid.

Title: “Bitter Christmas” Section: CompetitionDistributor: Sony Pictures ClassicsDirector: Pedro AlmodóvarBuzz: Almodóvar’s latest film curiously already opened to strong reviews in his native Spain back in March. A lush, colorful, and messy melodrama about pain and mourning sounds like an Amodóvar film to us.

Title: “Clarissa” Section: Director’s FortnightDistributor: NeonDirector: Arie Esiri and Chuko EsiriBuzz: The Nigerian directors behind “This Is My Desire” from 2020 team with Ayo Edebiri, David Oyelowo and Sophie Okonedo for a reimagining of Virginia Woolf’s “Ms. Dalloway” as set in Lagos.

Title: “Fatherland” Section: CompetitionDistributor: MUBIDirector: Pawel PawlikowskiBuzz: Polish director Pawlikowski’s first film in eight years since the searing “Cold War” is a docudrama about German author Thomas Mann in post-War Germany after having stood against the Nazis. Sandra Huller also stars.

Title: “Fjord” Section: CompetitionDistributor: NeonDirector: Cristian MungiuBuzz: Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve star in the latest film from Romanian auteur Mungiu, his first since 2022’s “R.M.N.,” which is about a Romanian immigrant family under scrutiny for investigation by the Norwegian government.

Title: “Her Private Hell” Section: Out of CompetitionDistributor: NeonDirector: Nicolas Winding RefnBuzz: “Her Private Hell” is “Drive” provocateur Nicolas Winding Refn’s first feature since 2016, and the film is a futuristic, fantastical story about a woman searching for her father and a soldier trying to recover his daughter from hell. #3511. Apple explains the $400 premium for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display

Apple argued that the touchscreen isn’t the headline feature of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, merely a bonus.

The headline should instead be the quality of the display itself – with the company effectively suggesting that the $400 premium is positively cheap for what you’re getting …

Apple published a white paper in which it argues that the latest MacBook Pro display is essentially a smaller version of its professional reference monitor, the Studio Display XDR.

$400 for the screen and new design isn’t my issue, my issue is the cost of storage and memory. $600 more to go from 24gb to 48gb or nearly a grand for 64gb. You can easily spend nearly double the cost of the machine just getting it to a semi-future proof spec.

Given that this costs anywhere from $2,899 to $3,599 just for a display (albeit a significantly larger one with a correspondingly higher resolution), this does put into perspective that $400 extra over the MacBook Pro with the standard screen. Here’s what Apple has to say about it:

PROLED XDR display, the best display in a pro laptop, finally overcomes these historic limitations. For the first time, a MacBook Pro display uses tandem OLED technology, delivering up to 1000 nits of sustained full-screen brightness, 2000 nits of peak high dynamic range (HDR) and standard dynamic range (SDR) brightness, and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with accurate, per-pixel black levels.

It’s driven in real time by an all-new display engine in M5 Pro and M5 Max, which continuously compensates each pixel for content, usage, temperature, and ambient conditions—delivering creative precision out of the box and protecting panel lifespan over time. And a unique manufacturing process ensures panel-to-panel consistency and minimizes off-axis color shift, a first for any OLED laptop.

As Macworld spotted, that’s almost identical to the company’s description of the the Studio Display XDR.

In fact, the PROLED XDR in the MacBook Pro is the only display other than the Studio Display XDR that supports Apple CMF 2026, the next generation of CIE 1931. Apple says CMF 2026 “more precisely aligns the appearance of the display with an ideal D65 illuminant—the standard reference for white—and significantly improves appearance matching across display technologies, which is important for workflows that use multiple displays side by side.”

Resolution aside, the other specs are identical with just one exception: the contrast ratio. As for that exception, the MacBook display comes out on top with a 10 million to 1 contrast ratio, in contrast with the Studio Display XDR’s one million.

Does this change your own perspective of the price premium of the OLED model? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3510. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3509. AI Movie ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Gets Serious with AI-Generated Grimes Cameo, Times Square Marketing Push, Oscar Screenings

When we first wrote about the coming release of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the first fully AI-generated feature film being self-distributed into movie theaters in the U.S., it would’ve been easy to write the whole thing off as a stunt.

Coming from YouTuber Gossip Goblin, who has an impressive and loyal following, “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” started earning comps from the press (and from the producers themselves) to the success Markiplier found when he self-released his film “Iron Lung” and made $50 million worldwide in the process. Would that success translate for an AI movie? A recent example from China suggests that may not be the case. Related Stories Cannes 2026 Movies Sold: Kino Lorber Buys Clio Barnard’s BIFA Contender ‘I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning’ Sony Pictures Classics Buys Jean-Pierre Jeunet’s ‘Violette’

It’s clear though the team behind “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is treating this like a real project that needs to be seen in theaters and is worthy of serious critical consideration, and they’re doing that with real marketing dollars behind its theatrical push.

Today, Gossip Goblin announced that pop star Grimes is set to make a cameo in his film “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” as is YouTuber Mike Majlak, and their involvement is being revealed via a massive Times Square ad campaign that is also launching today, all ahead of the film’s release next month on December 4. Gossip Goblin is even launching a contest for people to use AI to create their own short films within the universe of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” that can net the winning creator $15,000.

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” also sparked some headlines in the last few months with the news that the producers are plotting an Oscar campaign for Best Animated Feature. Turns out some FYC screenings have already started and a digital campaign begins at the end of November. All of the above suggests some real belief in the project, and with a collective 16 million views of the trailer thus far, they have reason to believe.

“We’ve been heartened already by the reaction,” producer Edward Saatchi of Fable Studios said in a statement. “One Oscar-Nominated animated film director compared ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ after seeing it to ‘2001,’ and we’ve had great feedback from Pixar folks (part of Fable’s team is ex-Pixar and we hugely respect their work).”

Zack London, the man behind the moniker Gossip Goblin, in speaking with IndieWire ahead of the announcement, said he’s “fully cognizant” of the controversy around putting a movie made with AI into theaters, and he acknowledges that all of this is “a big, unproven hypothesis.” But he says it would be “disingenuous to write it all off” as just an AI movie or not a real project.

Getting screens is easy, but the real battle is making people believe there are actually humans behind this movie, even if the images are all generated by AI. Roughly 30 to 35 people are credited in the making of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” and a behind-the-scenes documentary that is also in the works is aimed to humanize the process of making the movie. It includes interviews with the film’s composer and voice actors and shows its Foley guy doing real post-production work. Even the act of getting a real person like Grimes in the film — whose image is generated to resemble her but who does real voice acting — required an elaborate process of photo mashing atop existing character design to fit her into the movie, as well as contacting the model makers themselves to remove built-in censors for generating images of a public figure’s likeness.

On one hand, “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” can be viewed as a scrappy indie made by a team of creatives, not just a sole prompter working alone, making a movie that wouldn’t exist otherwise. On the other hand, many would argue that the visuals on display would normally require a team of thousands to bring to life along with millions of dollars. Depending on where you fall on that spectrum may determine whether you also buy a ticket to see it.

But London and Saatchi have grander ambitions with “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” and AI filmmaking beyond just what it can do at the box office. Saatchi says that for as many great CG animated films have been released in the last 30 years since “Toy Story” first hit theaters, they’ve arguably all looked similar and been made with the same techniques. He views “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” as the next “Toy Story” moment in animation, with a movie that aims to look psychedelic and otherworldly, something that looks unique and looks like it could only be the product of AI generative models. Other films may use AI to create something cheaply that looks like a Pixar movie, but London wanted to make something that looked like nothing else.

“Pixar set the look for animated films in the ’90s — they didn’t use technology to more cheaply make a film that looked like ‘Beauty and the Beast,’ they created a radically new aesthetic with ‘Toy Story,'” Saatchi said. “That’s what ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ represents: a wild new aesthetic for animated films that will define much of animated, actor-voiced films in the coming decades. This is that ‘Toy Story’ moment for our generation — a radical departure for animated films — you only need to see Grimes’ brilliant performance in the film to understand how much things are about to change for animated movies. And we hope the Academy will recognize that a film that is seminal (the first AI film), wildly technically novel and most importantly good deserves a nomination.”

#3507. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.
