#3506. Keanu Reeves' John Wick Prequel Movie Fate Finally Confirmed At Lionsgate

Keanu Reeves is definitely coming back for the new John Wick prequel movie.

Following his apparent departure from the franchise with Chapter 4's ending, discussions of a potential return from Reeves have swirled, with Lionsgate eventually announcing in April 2025 that both the animated prequel movie and a proper Chapter 5 were moving forward with him back as the iconic assassin. In the time since, it was also confirmed that Donnie Yen would be directing and starring in a Caine spinoff movie, which wrapped production in July 2026.

Nearly two years after the studio previously confirmed its plans to produce the project, Lionsgate's latest earnings call has confirmed the fate of Reeves' John Wick animated prequel movie, giving it the official greenlight, and putting it currently in the pre-production stage. The film is being helmed by Ultraman: Rising's Shannon Tindle, while Ryan and Kaz Firpo are attached to pen the script.

Development on the animated John Wick prequel movie has been in the works for the better part of three years, with franchise boss Chad Stahelski announcing plans for it in late 2023 and teasing it being done in an anime styling. However, at the time, he indicated that it was going to be a TV series, and didn't originally describe it as being a direct prequel centered on Reeves' eponymous character, with 2025's CinemaCon bringing the latter reveal.

The project's previous announcement did also come with the reveal that the animated John Wick prequel movie would explore the iconic Impossible Task teased in the previous movies that he completed in order to effectively retire from the High Table-run world for a life with his soulmate, Helen. It has not yet been made clear if this will result in other returning characters being featured in the film, namely Willem Dafoe's Marcus, Michael Nyqvist's Viggo or Bridget Moynahan as Helen.

One notable change to come from the official Lionsgate greenlight is that the John Wick prequel movie has shifted its writing team. The film was originally set to be penned by Game of Thrones and The Shape of Water alum Vanessa Taylor, only for the Firpo cousins, who previously developed the screen story and a draft of the screenplay for Marvel's Eternals movie, to now be attached.

#3504. The 6 Best Thrillers Released Between 2020 and Now

The thrill of a thriller is how the story makes you feel. A great thriller film relies on sustained tension, high stakes, and constant uncertainty that keeps you on the edge of your seat. A great thriller works by manipulating how and when the audience learns crucial information. Often featuring tight editing, sharp sound design, dim lighting, and deliberate pacing to suffocate the comfort zone and build toward a memorable climax, a thriller becomes legendary when it leaves a lasting impression.

The 21st century has provided some extraordinary entries within the genre, but this current decade seems to be turning into a profound golden age. Since 2020, the thriller has become brilliantly risky, mixing big-budget masterpieces with mind-blowing indie projects that have altered the landscape. With so many brilliant films over the last six years, the six on this list have emerged as the very best. From game-changing horror thrillers to psychological dramas that mess with your mind, these six films became instant classics the moment they were released. What’s your favorite thriller of the 2020s?

In the highly underrated Pig, directed by Michael Sarnoski, Rob Feld (Nicolas Cage) is a reclusive truffle hunter living in the Oregon wilderness whose beloved foraging pig is suddenly stolen. To rescue her, he must return to his past life in the Portland culinary scene and confront the grief he left behind. It is a quiet, meditative drama about loss, artistic expression, and connection, not a traditional revenge thriller. By subverting genre tropes, Pig became the antithesis of thrillers, honing in on themes of authenticity and the power of connection.

Initially set up to look like a gritty "John Wick with a pig," where a hermit tracks down his stolen pet, the film abandons blood and retribution in favor of deep conversations and emotional vulnerability. Cage delivers a grounded, mournful, and restrained performance, moving into a new chapter of his storied career. The dynamic between Rob and his young, status-obsessed truffle buyer Amir (Alex Wolff) acts as a mirror for both to face their traumas head-on. The film becomes a poetic examination of how people process loss, regret, and the difference between fake artifice and genuine passion. Pig is a mesmerizing and moving story of love and loss that redefined how a thriller can be presented. ​​​​​​​

Don’t sleep on foreign films! The 2020s have seen a rise of foreign films finding their way into the Hollywood mainstream. Such was the case for Anatomy of a Fall. Directed by Justine Triet, the psychological courtroom thriller follows Sandra Voyter (Sandra Hüller), a German writer accused of murdering her French husband, Samuel Maleski (Samuel Theis), after he falls to his death from their secluded alpine chalet. With their visually impaired son, Daniel Maleski (Milo Machado-Graner), as the sole witness, the trial transforms from a forensic investigation into an intense, public dissection of the couple's turbulent marriage and conflicting realities. Ultimately, Anatomy of a Fall explores the ambiguous boundaries of truth, language, and memory when a relationship is put on trial.

The film emerged as a legal and psychological thriller because it treats the "truth" as an elusive, multi-layered question rather than a simple puzzle to be solved. It turns a murder investigation into a surgical dissection of an ordinary, flawed, and decaying relationship. Through the ambiguity of truth, the narrative explores how personal history, bias, and fiction can be weaponized in a courtroom. The film put the sensational Hüller on the map thanks to her stoic, razor-sharp, and deeply vulnerable performance. Earning the Palme d'Or at Cannes, Anatomy of a Fall strips away genre clichés to offer a haunting look at how private grief is put on public trial.

You’ll never look at your food the same after watching The Menu. Directed by Mark Mylod and written by Seth Reiss and Will Tracy, the film follows a young couple, Tyler (Nicholas Hoult) and Margot (Anya Taylor-Joy), and a group of ultra-wealthy elites who travel to a remote island to dine at an exclusive restaurant. The evening takes a sinister turn as the enigmatic celebrity chef, Chef Slowik (Ralph Fiennes), reveals that each conceptual course is part of a calculated, deadly plan to punish his pretentious guests. The Menu serves as a sharp satire on class divide, foodie culture, and the exploitation of the service industry.

The Menu stands out as an acid-tongued examination of the pretentious, hyper-exclusive fine-dining industry, using it as a microcosm to skewer classism, economic inequality, and the vanity of the ultra-wealthy. Set almost entirely on a remote private island, the movie builds claustrophobic, uninterrupted tension where every course on the menu escalates the dread. With biting thrills and shocking twists, The Menu delivers a delicious dish in which the audience laughs wholly at absurd foodie culture one moment and feels genuinely disturbed the next. Fiennes commands the screen as the terrifying, cult-leader-like Chef Slowik, while Taylor-Joy masters the grounded outsider who becomes the beacon of promise. The Menu brilliantly keeps you off-guard until the very last dish is presented. ​​​​​​​

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what it would leave behind.

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever won that particular argument.

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

A masterclass in modernizing a classic text, The Invisible Man brings fear, terror, and profound social commentary. Written and directed by Leigh Whannell, The Invisible Man tells the story of Cecilia Kass (Elisabeth Moss) as she escapes her abusive, wealthy optics scientist boyfriend, Adrian Griffin (Oliver Jackson-Cohen). After Adrian seemingly commits suicide, Cecilia becomes convinced she is being stalked and terrorized by an unseen, invisible force. With no one else believing her claims, she must fight independently to uncover the deadly truth and save herself. The Invisible Man earns its honorable reputation by transforming a classic sci-fi monster tale into a tense, grounded study of domestic abuse and gaslighting.

Instead of focusing on the mad scientist, the narrative centers on the victim. It mirrors the psychological isolation of real-world coercive control and gaslighting, where no one believes that an abuser is still haunting you. Whannell frequently frames Cecilia off-center in wide shots, leaving empty hallways and seemingly vacant rooms on screen, forcing you to scan the background, generating constant paranoia and suspense. Moss delivers an intensely physical performance, reacting to empty space, silent dread, and invisible physical force with visceral realism. It’s one of her best performances to date. The film is a masterclass in thrills, putting Whannell on the visionary map. ​​​​​​​

2026 is the year of low-budget horror masterpieces. Leading the charge is the incomparable Obsession. Written and directed by Curry Barker, the story follows a socially awkward man named Bear Bailey (Michael Johnston) who uses a cursed novelty toy called the One Wish Willow to force his coworker crush, Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette), to fall in love with him. While his wish initially seems to come true, Nikki's affection quickly warps into an extreme, violent, and terrifyingly possessive fixation. As the supernatural compulsion takes over, Bear finds himself trapped in a dangerous nightmare of his own making that escalates into fatal consequences. Earning itself a spot as a towering cinematic phenomenon, Obsession brilliantly injects terror into a seemingly basic "be careful what you wish for" setup.

Shot on a microbudget, Obsession shocked the world by grossing over $500 million worldwide. The viral word-of-mouth campaign worked as audiences were taken by the brilliant premise and conversations it sparked. On the surface, the film plays with a classic Faustian premise that becomes a brutal critique of male entitlement. The true psychological horror doesn't come from a masked killer, but from Bear’s willingness to strip away Nikki's autonomy and stay with her terrifying, cursed doppelgänger just to preserve his own wish-fulfillment fantasy. The film’s instant legendary status was earned through the dynamic duo of Johnston and Navarette. Barker builds suspense through classic tricks and craftsmanship. The boxed-in frame physically traps the audience with the characters, amplifying the intense feelings of domestic captivity and dread. It’s a masterclass in making silence itself feel threatening, using subtle tonality shifts and unsettling audio rumbles to make viewers physically uncomfortable. Obsession continues the trend of new voices and faces reshaping the genre's landscape. ​​​​​​​

One of the most groundbreaking and masterful thrillers in decades, Weapons is sheer brilliance. Written and directed by Zach Cregger, the supernatural mystery-horror thriller centers on a small town thrown into chaos after seventeen third-grade children from the same classroom inexplicably vanish into the dark at exactly 2:17 AM. The story utilizes a non-linear, multi-perspective narrative to follow a pariah teacher, Justine Gandy (Julia Garner), a grieving father, Archer Graff (Josh Brolin), and other local figures as they unearth a sinister web of blood rituals, police corruption, and witchcraft. Beneath its terrifying mystery is a story centered on the eccentric Aunt Gladys (Amy Madigan). Weapons serves as a deeper, personal allegory exploring generational trauma, grief, and the destructive nature of addiction.

In a time when franchises and blockbusters dominated Hollywood, Weapons delivered something genuinely ambitious, unnerving, and profound. Cregger weaves an intricate web across six distinct chapters, building tension purely through withheld information. Shot by cinematographer Larkin Seiple, the film utilizes constant, creeping tracking shots and slow zooms that refuse to let the audience look away. The claustrophobic nature is matched by a haunting sound design, generating visceral dread even when the horrors occur entirely off-screen. The film effortlessly balances bleak, psychological terror with sharp, pitch-black humor. Its tonal agility lets it shift from pure terror to surreal absurdity without ever breaking its spell. The film earned high honors thanks to Madigan’s iconic performance. She ensured Aunt Gladys earned a spot in the horror villain hall of fame. Weapons is a thriller masterpiece that became the new gold standard.

#3501. ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

Among the bleakest films ever made, Werner Herzog’s “Stroszek” (1977) famously ends not with the suicide of its title character, but with a haunting coda in which a chicken pecks at a miniature piano inside a surreal roadside tourist trap’s coin-operated display. It’s a visual metaphor for the inescapable banality of life on Earth, and for the dehumanizing work people are forced to do to disguise the many failures of the American Dream. It’s also the last thing that Joy Division frontman Ian Curtis saw before he killed himself. “Look into the eyes of a chicken,” Herzog has said, “and you will see real stupidity. It is a kind of bottomless stupidity, a fiending stupidity. They are the most horrifying, cannibalistic, and nightmarish creatures in the world.” Related Stories Robert Pattinson to Receive 2026 American Cinematheque Award AI Movie ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Gets Serious with AI-Generated Grimes Cameo, Times Square Marketing Push, Oscar Screenings

That sentiment has long endured as modern cinema’s definitive stance on chickens (despite Aardman’s best efforts), but now, after witnessing the 50 years of entropy that followed “Stroszek,” Hungarian filmmaker György Pálfi is crying fowl. Chickens are not the most horrifying, cannibalistic, and nightmarish creatures in the world, he contends. We are. How can you tell? Easy: Just look at us through the eyes of a chicken.

A cute, cockeyed yarn that unspools like a feathered cross between “EO” and “Flow,” Pálfi’s “Hen” tells the story of a jet-black Leghorn chicken who escapes a Greek factory farm after she’s plucked from the rest of her flock because of the color of her plumage. A worker decides to take the bird home so that his wife can serve it for dinner, but our sly heroine — played by a brave hen named Feri, in addition to her seven indistinguishable stunt doubles — makes a daring escape when her captor stops his truck to refuel. But she’s snapped up again by the teeth of a dog named Titan, who carries the chicken back to the ramshackle seaside restaurant where his owner (Yannis Kokiasmenos) has much bigger problems than what to serve for dinner.

If the precise contours of those problems are a bit difficult to deduce, that’s probably because — as we’ve already established — this movie is told through the eyes of a chicken. Sometimes literally, thanks to Pálfi’s judicious deployment of POV, which is useful for times when our ruffled protagonist is, say, trapped inside a cardboard box (there’s an excellent bit where the hen starts moving the cardboard box from the inside, a “Metal Gear Solid”-inspired visual gag that proves typical of the director’s wry humor). And what does a chicken know of Europe’s ongoing migrant crisis? Of a protest between angry citizens and riot police? Of human trafficking, and the complications thereof? To judge by the film’s regular assortment of amusingly blank reaction shots, I’d wager “very little.” The titular hen doesn’t even think to look both ways when she crosses the road after flying the coop, let alone have a good answer as to why she’s doing it.

For the most part, the hen is focused on clucking her neck, surviving the pecking order at the restaurant farm where she winds up, and potentially even laying a few eggs of her own someday (we see her hatch in the movie’s first scene, but they grow up so fast). Most of the human drama is relegated to the distant background, as Pálfi mines the humor from his movie’s conceit by using the restaurant as a lens onto the hen’s predicament rather than the other way around. The people are mere archetypes, but some of the animals we meet appear so layered and inscrutable that you’d happily watch a three-hour Nathan Fielder documentary about them. (The terse and fiery courtship between the star hen and her most aggressive suitor is soundtracked by a classic Greek love song, a flourish that stands out in a film where desperate migrants are being left for dead just off-camera.)

Then again, couldn’t every film about — and starring — real live animals be considered a documentary to some extent? Feri the chicken has been trained by the best of the business, but she remains blissfully unaware of the camera, and Pálfi takes pains not to anthropomorphize her any more than necessary. Plenty of heightened enjoyment comes elsewhere, much of it laundered through Giorgos Karvelas’ saturated cinematography, Szabolcs Szoke’s hyper-dynamic score, and the furtive way Pálfi bends the film’s crafts into something that almost resembles a chicken’s idea of a Western.

Here, the hen is a hen is a hen, and while “Hen” is prone to long and repetitive stretches in which she basically just hens around as a result of that approach, the animal’s natural obliviousness is too crucial a contrast to our own willful antipathy for Pálfi to risk muddying the difference between the two. At the risk of making the movie’s side-eyed social commentary sound more didactic than it is in practice (save for one very pointed moment towards the end that explicitly affirms Herzog’s claim), “Hen” uses a chicken’s lack of moral responsibility to highlight the mandate we have to heed our own, no matter how effectively we’ve evolved to ignore it.

No matter how good we get at farming other species, and killing our own. Pálfi does very little to goose or otherwise manipulate our emotional attachment to his chicken star, but there’s still something to be said for how easily we become more invested in this witless hen’s fate than in that of the doomed people with whom she crosses paths. By the time it reaches its end, this strange but sober film starts to point back to the beginning, cutting from a single egg being squeezed out of a hen’s vent (Google says “vent”) to a vast sea of them bobbling around inside the factory’s machines. One is easy to follow, and to care about. Thousands are a statistic. We’re smart enough to farm other animals, but people — like chickens — won’t hesitate to eat each other the minute they get hungry.

Dekanalog will release “Hen” in theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3499. John Ternus talks plans to improve Siri AI

During Apple’s quarterly earnings call, CEO John Ternus was asked repeatedly about Siri AI’s future. Here’s what he said about Apple’s plans for improving and expanding Siri AI.

Sometimes when Apple launches a new feature or product, the company sees its work as finished, and whatever ships goes unchanged for far too long. Many might characterize Siri this way, arguing the assistant went years without meaningful improvement or updates.

But according to Apple CEO John Ternus, the Siri AI that just shipped is only the beginning of what’s planned.

Yesterday on Apple’s quarterly earnings call, Ternus gave a rundown of Siri AI’s capabilities. He concluded: “We’re really excited to have rolled all these innovations out, and there’s still so much more we plan to do.”

This signals that Apple doesn’t see Siri AI as a feature that can now be left alone for a while. Instead, as we already saw in iOS 27.2 last week, Apple is focused on rapidly improving it.

Now that Siri AI is out, I would like to see it iterate as follows:

Support for a wider range of file types, such as PDF.

Accessing it from Search (especially on the Mac) should be instantaneous and reliable.

Proactively suggesting and reminding the user based on what it knows.

What are those future plans? It sounds like agentic capabilities may be among them. Ternus said:

With Siri AI, we really have the kind of—the Siri we always wanted. It’s primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it’s built on a modern, orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand capabilities over time.

It’s telling that Ternus says Siri is “primarily request-based today” and mentions “room to expand capabilities” before pivoting to mention agentic features. It sounds like Apple is already, behind-the-scenes, envisioning and working toward a version of Siri that won’t need to be “primarily request-based.”

Finally, later in the call when discussing opportunities for services growth, including potentially launching new services, Ternus says: “We think intelligence is going to be another opportunity as well.” This refers back to an earlier discussion of Apple’s intent to charge a fee for expanded usage limits on certain Siri AI and Apple Intelligence capabilities. The idea is that as Siri evolves and improves, Apple will have opportunities to charge for certain features.

What are your takeaways from Ternus’s comments on Siri AI? Let us know in the comments.

#3498. Sam Winchester’s New Supernatural Spinoff Is 5-Star Perfection

As much as I love Sam Winchester, I had my reservations about diving into a Supernatural spin-off without Dean Winchester (what can I say? I'm a ride-or-die Dean girl through and through). But after its second release, Sam's new spin-off series is officially in full swing, and I can confidently say I'm hooked.

If you haven’t been keeping up with all things Supernatural, you may not know that, despite The CW's Supernatural ending with a devastating series finale, the franchise has experienced a major revival at Dynamite Entertainment. The publisher has launched several canon-compliant Supernatural comic series, all set during the show's earlier seasons.

Matthew Lillard is officially returning as Shaggy in a new Scooby-Doo series in 2027, marking a dream comeback for longtime fans.

In 2025, Dynamite launched its now-concluded 10-issue Supernatural series by Greg Pak. Following this flagship series, the publisher released Supernatural Special: Wayward, which set the stage for what is quickly becoming the franchise's most ambitious chapter yet. What makes this new era so ambitious is that it has separated the Winchester brothers, giving each of them their own ongoing series: Supernatural: Dean Winchester and Supernatural: Sam Winchester.

Both series launched in early October and dropped their second issues this past Wednesday. While I was immediately hooked on Chuck Brown and Rapha Lobosco's first issue of Dean Winchester, I was still relatively unsure about Paulina Ganucheau and Kendall Goode's Sam Winchester #1, thanks to what felt like a slow start. However, the second issue delivered on everything the first had set up and has officially earned a five-star rating from me.

Those who read Supernatural Special: Wayward know that the brothers went their separate ways after Sam began receiving mysterious calls and texts warning him that Dean would die if he didn't abandon his brother. Unwilling to risk his brother's life, Sam eventually runs away from Dean and sets out to hunt alone. This premise sets up both series, and in Supernatural: Sam Winchester, we see Sam continue to be hounded by his mysterious caller as he investigates a strange farmhouse in the middle of nowhere.

While issue #1 didn't exactly wow me, I went into issue #2 with extremely high expectations thanks to its synopsis, which teased the arrival of the legendary cryptid Mothman. Needless to say, I was not disappointed. Here, some of the mystery established in the first issue finally begins to unravel, with the story seemingly suggesting that Sam's mysterious caller is actually the legendary Mothman, or at least connected to the creature in some way.

Goode does a 10/10 job bringing Mothman to life, delivering an eerie and unique interpretation of the legendary cryptid through his art. However, it's the humor and character revelations Ganucheau brings to this issue that ultimately earned it five stars from me. First, Mothman essentially demands that Sam care for the little girl he found in the farmhouse's basement. Having Sam unexpectedly become a guardian to a little girl introduces an interesting dynamic that wasn't explored in the TV series.

What's more, Sam seeing similarities between the girl and his brother helps keep one of the franchise's defining themes intact, even with the Winchesters separated: Sam and Dean's unconditional love for each other. Although Dean isn't physically present in the narrative, his presence is constantly felt through Sam's thoughts and actions, making this feel like a genuine Supernatural story.

Furthermore, Mothman's insistence that Sam keep the little girl safe also suggests that our initial assumption about the mysterious caller being the villain might not be entirely correct. Something else is clearly going on here, and the possibility that the caller isn't quite as sinister as we initially thought adds another intriguing layer to the mystery. It's this kind of supernatural intrigue, where things aren't always as straightforward as they seem, that helped define The CW series, and I'm thrilled to see it making its way into these comics.

The story also gets some much-appreciated humor from the mysterious caller, which is slowly humanizing the character. For example, the caller chastising Sam for not charging his phone was one of the issue's dialogue highlights, as was the mystery caller calling Sam a "good boy" when he followed their instructions. These little moments add a surprising amount of personality to an otherwise unsettling presence, making me even more curious about who (or what) is on the other end of that phone.

So, if you haven't yet dived into Supernatural: Sam Winchester, or you stopped early after issue #1, consider this your sign to give the series another shot. It's clear that Ganucheau and Goode are only just getting started, and if this second issue is any indication, they could be building something truly special. As a longtime Supernatural fan who initially wasn't sure how I'd feel about a Sam-focused story without Dean, I couldn't be happier to be proven wrong.

Six years after Supernatural ended, a new Dean Winchester series pushes the franchise forward, but its latest chapter leaves Jensen Ackles behind.

Supernatural: Sam Winchester #2 from Dynamite is now available!

#3497. ‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups

There are dozens of scenes that capture “North of North’s” digestible, defiant kindness, but my favorite arrives near the start of the second season’s second episode. Siaja (Anna Lambe) wakes up, grabs a glass of water, and promptly spits it out. The local water supply is contaminated (“They must’ve cranked those chemicals again,” her mom says), so Siaja heads to the nearest store to load up on jugs of clean water. Outside, there’s an elderly woman perched on her snowmobile, smoking a cigarette, who loudly hassles Siaja for a little charity.

“Must be nice,” the woman shouts, getting Siaja’s attention. “[You] buying filtered water. It’s too expensive [for me]. [I] gotta drink government pool water. Back in the day, we had nice ice straight from the river. Pure, nice, and healthy.” Related Stories ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken ‘Black Doves’ Review: Season 2 Sticks to Its Guns in Keira Knightley’s Excellent, Existential Spy Thriller

On that last word, “healthy,” the woman takes a drag from her cigarette, and while she’s doubled over coughing, Siaja takes her forceful hint and puts one of her water jugs in the woman’s cart. “Here, you take this,” Siaja says. The woman, speaking in Inuktitut, does not say “thank you”; she asks if she can keep the jug. Then she hacks a loogie into the snow as Siaja drives off, punctuating just how little the gesture means to her.

Now, it’s clear this woman knows exactly what she’s doing. She didn’t end up outside the town’s only source for clean water by accident, and Siaja knows it. But she also knows the woman is telling the truth: She’s too old to get ice for herself, and she’s too poor to afford purified water. Siaja also knows this woman is her elder, and elders should be taken care of. So after acquiescing in the moment, Siaja expands on the idea soon after: She grabs Alistair (Jay Ryan), her big, burly dad, and they go get blocks of ice from the river to deliver around town — for free.

Of course, it doesn’t go exactly as planned (the rivers aren’t all “pure” and “healthy” anymore), but Siaja’s chance encounter with the woman serves as the impetus for the entire episode: Siaja uses it to prove to her boss that she can be more than an assistant at the community center. She bonds with her dad, who she’s still getting to know. She sets a good example for her daughter, Bun (Keira Belle Cooper), and she still finds time to flirt with her crush, Kuuk (Braeden Clarke), in between deliveries.

Siaja is doing exactly what she set out to do from the start of the season: “level up” her life.

Reading it back now, the story sounds corny. But despite all that positive energy driving so many warm-hearted gestures, “North by North” never becomes saccharine. Siaja’s triumphs don’t feel like cheap schmaltz. They hit that tricky TV sweet spot, where characters’ helpful actions and benevolent intentions feel genuine even when, on paper, they seem too nice to be tolerable.

It helps, of course, that Siaja fucks up early and often. Nothing makes a win land like taking many embarrassing losses to get there, as she did in Season 1 after summoning the courage to leave her husband, get a job, and start fresh — with an adorable daughter in tow. In Season 2, her plan to charm tourists doesn’t go over as whimsically as she imagined. Her plan to get her own place doesn’t include dropping in the rankings on an endless waiting list for affordable housing. Her plan to ditch her small-minded ex-husband (who doesn’t appear in Season 2) doesn’t include sitting for rounds of speed-dating or waiting out a relationship that may never end.

Siaja’s self-actualization isn’t as easy as ditching the zero to get with the hero, even when she’s her own hero from the jump — it takes time to learn the ins and outs of public service, to connect with people, and to make sense of your own emotions. “North of North” respects each process while savoring her struggle through them. (Lambe’s comic timing remains pitch-perfect, and her ability to navigate tonal swings is just as sharp.)

Investing in Siaja’s incremental progress does wonders to keep “North of North” from feeling like forgettable fluff — especially when the back-half of Season 2 gets heavy wrestling with familial, cultural, and communal responsibilities — but none of it work without the attention to detail surrounding Siaja, too. When the first season premiered in January 2025, “North by North” earned plenty of well-deserved praise for its authenticity. The fictional town of Ice Cove represents real communities in Nunavet, the northernmost part of Canada within the Arctic Circle, and the series employed a heavily Indigenous cast and crew to help bring it to life.

And what life there is: Season 2 is rich with cultural specifics, from a Greenlandic mask-dancing celebration to public safety concerns. (Beyond the bad water, don’t forget to place your beer orders early! A birthday without a brewski could be your last!) Every episode whisks you away to a very cold, very kind small town, which is oh-so-welcoming on chilly winter evenings when you just want to bask in the season’s cozy glow.

Respecting and highlighting Inuk customs is step one. Step two expands the idea by grounding “North by North” in perspectives beyond their beloved lead screwup. That way, her work ethic and generosity stay sweet and meaningful (when overexposure could easily turn them sour) and the show’s overall tone avoids becoming rote. Siaja’s mom, Neevee (Maika Harper), is the sardonic balance her daughter demands, and how they flesh out her backstory to explain her sharp disposition offers some of the season’s strongest scenes. Helen (Mary Lynn Rajskub), Siaja’s boss, is an oblivious white lady desperate to be cherished as a leader, and her pushy ambitions help clarify Siaja’s unselfish aid to others (while generating laughs).

And then there’s the townsfolk, who may not always be as colorful as the woman demanding free water, but who share her fair yet formidable spirit. If Siaja’s community service was met with cheers and applause, it would be unbelievable. That’s not how citizens treat their local officials. But their measured disposition isn’t just authentic, it’s essential. Similarly, if the citizens were the butt of every joke (like in “Parks and Recreation”), Siaja’s dedication could feel misplaced. If they were mean, like too many real-life city council visitors, her above-and-beyond gestures could seem foolish. Instead, Siaja’s community is just there, living their own lives, waiting for her to get her shit together and do what’s right by them.

“North of North” Season 2 premieres Thursday, November 5 on Netflix. All eight episodes will be released at once.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3495. Apple Wallet driver’s licenses coming to three new states soon

Apple Wallet driver’s licenses recently launched in Virginia and Oklahoma, but three more states are expected to follow soon, bringing us close to 20 US states on board.

Digital IDs are becoming far more common than they were when Apple first added support in the Wallet app back in 2021. And today, 16 US states plus Puerto Rico support the feature on iPhone.

The latest additions, Virginia and Oklahoma, debuted just in the last couple months.

And it looks like three more states will be coming soon:

This summer evidence was discovered of both Utah and Virginia being added to Apple’s backend for driver’s license support. Virginia has since gone live, so it’s expected that Utah will launch as one of the next supported states.

Kentucky previously announced it will support Apple Wallet driver’s licenses after upgrading its digital ID system this summer. All indications are that the upgrade has been completed, so based on the state’s original plans, we should see licenses in Apple Wallet soon.

North Carolina recently announced the launch of its new digital driver’s license system. As part of the announcement, it confirmed licenses will be supported in Apple Wallet by early 2027.

Additional states might always surprise us and launch in Wallet before Utah, Kentucky, or North Carolina. We’ve seen a clear acceleration of states signing on to offer Wallet driver’s licenses.

But for now at least, the three states above appear the strongest candidates to debut soon.

For more info on states that have pledged Apple Wallet support, see our coverage here.

#3494. Keanu Reeves Officially Returns for New John Wick Prequel

John Wick is back...but maybe not in the way you might have expected. Keanu Reeves will return as cinema's deadliest assassin in a new prequel film detailing a key moment in his life before his movie franchise began. And don't worry about having to de-age Keanu with CG, because that won't be necessary.

John Wick exploded into theaters in 2014, vaulting star Reeves into the upper echelons of action stardom. Reeves starred as the retired assassin of the title, who returned to his old ways when his dog, the last gift from his late wife, was callously killed by the upstart heir to a criminal empire. After killing his way to the top, Wick soon found himself entrapped in the assassin life once more in a series of sequels, hunted by every other hitman and bounty hunter on Earth before seemingly going to his final rest in 2022's John Wick: Chapter 4. However, he still managed to find time to appear in the spin-off movie Ballerina, set before that film, in which he faced off with the title character, played by Ana de Armas.

Lionsgate has greenlit an animated John Wick movie, in which Reeves will reprise his role as the iconic assassin. But don't expect to find out how (or if) Wick survived his apparent demise at the conclusion of John Wick 4. The movie will be a prequel that will explore Wick's life before he gave up the assassin life and retired, as we first met him in the original John Wick. It will detail how he accomplished the so-called 'Impossible Task" that allowed him to escape the all-consuming criminal underworld and retire to be with his beloved wife, Helen. The film is set to be directed by Shannon Tindle (Ultraman: Rising), from a script by Ryan and Kaz Firpo (Eternals). Reeves and Chad Stahelski, who directed all four previous Wick movies, will executive produce with Thunder Road’s Basil Iwanyk and Erica Lee.

Four action series. One of them is built around exactly the way you handle pressure, people, and a room that has just gone very quiet. Here is where you would survive the trilogy, and probably headline it.

You are precision with a grudge. You don't posture, you don't escalate, and you don't warn anybody twice. That is exactly why the people who know you are so careful never to be the reason you start.

You understand the thing the whole franchise is secretly about: the cars are spectacular, but the crew is the point. You collect people, you keep them, and you'd drive through a building for any one of them.

You over-prepare and then take the dangerous part yourself anyway. It looks like control, but it's really responsibility. You have never worked out how to ask somebody else to carry the risk.

You are not the most trained person in the building, the best equipped, or the one anybody would have picked. You are simply the one still standing at the end, which turns out to be the only qualification that matters.

John Wick will return in John Wick 5; Reeves has signed on to star, but details about that film are being kept at the High Table for the time being. However, one other spin-off is well underway: Caine, starring Donnie Yen as the blind swordsman of the title who aided Wick in John Wick 4, completed filming last summer. Yen also directs the film, which stars Rina Sawayama, Dacre Montgomery, Mason Thames, Bill Nighy, and Zhuang Dafei.

An animated John Wick movie is in development; no release date has yet been announced. Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

#3493. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3492. iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving

iOS 27.2 arrived last week with a variety of new features and changes for iPhone. Here are two new iOS 27.2 features I’ve been loving lately.

I’ve used Apple Podcasts for the last few years after previously sticking with third-party apps. The native Podcasts app won me over with excellent features like transcripts and automatic chapters.

My main hesitation in recommending the Podcasts app, however, has been its confusing Up Next queue. Thankfully, iOS 27.2 delivers a long-awaited fix.

In iOS 27.2, the Home tab in Apple Podcasts splits Up Next into two separate sections: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

These new sections offer, in my view, a much better system than what was there before. I no longer lose track of episodes I’ve previously started, since they’re not getting replaced by new episodes in my queue. Instead, there’s a clear divide between what’s new and what’s in-progress.

Shared Albums have long been one of my favorite features in Apple Photos. I don’t post on social media often, but I do love sharing photos and videos with close family and friends via the Photos app.

iOS 27 brought big upgrades to Shared Albums, the first notable changes in years. And to my surprise, Apple has already introduced even more improvements with iOS 27.2. Per Apple:

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos

Support for editing captions and comments is long overdue, but a welcome addition. I also love the prompt that helps prevent duplicate photos, because I always find myself needing to double-check if I’ve shared certain photos already—now I don’t have to anymore.

#3491. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3490. ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 3, 2026 during the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

Another melancholically splenetic Martin McDonagh jag about a banter-mad pair of murderers who go on a boys trip to purgatory (where they search their souls as they wait for death to find them), the prickly but unconvincing “Wild Horse Nine” strains to translate the post-Guy Ritchie bark of “In Bruges” into the language of a classic American Western. In this case, an American Western set on Easter Island and backdropped by Augusto Pinochet’s rise to power in the fall of 1973.  Related Stories ‘North of North’ Season 2 Review: Netflix’s Defiantly Nice Arctic Sitcom Is for the Warmhearted F**k-Ups ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

McDonagh’s decision to recast his same old script against the backdrop of such a real and terrible event grants this new telling a welcome sense of scale, both in terms of its characters’ morality, as well as in regards to their greater place in history. But that decision is a double-edged sword that cuts the film off at the knees. Where “In Bruges” kicked off with the killing of a fictional altar boy, “Wild Horse Nine” is overshadowed by the deaths of thousands upon thousands of very real people, and that reality bleeds into the edges of the frame even when the seriocomic absurdity of McDonagh’s writing demands a world of pure invention.

Does the overlap make “Wild Horse Nine” feel glib? Yes, and thank god for that — if not for glibness the movie would lose the majority of its few solid laughs. The problem is that it also makes “Wild Horse Nine” feel as transparently manufactured as the CIA-backed overthrow of a foreign democracy. I can accept that an inexperienced hitman might have a dark night of the soul after shooting an innocent child during confession. By contrast, I struggle to believe that a veteran CIA agent who openly brags about his involvement in the Kennedy assassination would have a come-to-Jesus moment after orchestrating the demise of Salvador Allende. McDonagh has some good fun wrestling with whether or not we should care about such a mottled change of heart, but the point is gradually rendered moot in a movie whose emotions are less credible than its conspiracies.

The original Company man, Chris (John Malkovich, more locked in than he’s been on screen since “Burn After Reading”) is a natural hinge for the off-kilter comedy that McDonagh builds around him, in that he can be a joy to watch even when you don’t buy a word he’s saying. More than just an ordinary CIA agent, he’s the living personification of America’s efforts to destabilize foreign governments across the 20th century. He was close with Patrice Lumumba until the day the Congolese leader was executed by a firing squad. He was in Cuba to spur on the exiles who failed to overthrow Fidel Castro in 1961. He was even in Dallas, USA on a Friday afternoon in November 1963, doing things his ornery boss MJ (Steve Buscemi) would much prefer he didn’t tell you about.

He traveled to all of those places, and got all of those people killed, with the blithe imperiousness of a flag waving in the wind. Chris says that he’s killed 68 people over the course of his career, and he offers that information as easily as a rumor — in a way that makes it sound like the number could be half that, or double, and it wouldn’t make a difference.

Recently, fate has blown Chris and his office husband/platonic life partner/exasperated straightman Lee (McDonagh vet Sam Rockwell) down south to Chile, where the two of them have been hard at work orchestrating the September 11th coup against the democratically elected socialist president, knowing full well that it would plunge the country into decades of brutal dictatorship. Chris appears to delight in sowing chaos, and the fact that he gets to wear a cute little Panama hat while he does it only boosts his joie de vivre.

But Chris is fraying at the seams in ways that we can’t see at first — ways that will only begin to reveal themselves when he and Lee decide to celebrate their imminent success with a sightseeing trip to Easter Island, a short 2,300 miles off the Western coast of Santiago. There are still a couple of months to go before the coup, but the wheels are in motion, and there’s little for these men to do for now besides fly to Rapa Nui, look at the “big heads,” flirt with a couple of beautiful young leftists (the prissier but gentler of whom is played by “Ema” mega-talent Mariana di Girolamo), and mordantly reflect upon their role in the awfulness Pinochet will soon inflict upon his own people. That task is complicated and confused by the fact that Chris seems to be losing his memory, which casts Lee in the role of his peevish but loving caretaker.

“Wild Horse Nine” is only the second feature that’s ever been shot on the ultra-remote soil of Rapa Nui (Kevin Reynolds’ 1994 epic “Rapa Nui” is credited as the first), and McDonagh rightly exalts in the fact that he’s brought Hollywood to the end of the world. The first half of his movie largely adheres to the fiction that Chris and Lee are just on Easter Island to fuck around, which offers a semi-relaxed opportunity for us to take in the sights. Ben Davis’ sun-bleached cinematography renders the hills and beaches of Rapa Nui with the veneer of a lost idyll, the ancient moai statues assuming an especially sacred charge when contrasted against such profane characters.

Chris bemusedly laughs the statues off with ethnographic glee, mocking one of the shorter figures as a dwarf (in case the “In Bruges” déjà vu wasn’t already strong enough), but it’s clear that he’s shaken by the fact that some of them almost 750 years old. That they’ve stood there in silent tribute to Polynesia’s ancestors as empires rose and fell on faraway shores, each of them a graveyard of forgotten people just like him. By the same token, it’s similarly clear that he’s trying to get at something in his own mind as he and Lee listen to Judy Collins in their rental car, argue over whether or not any Nazis made it into heaven (among other even more aggressively screen-written subjects), and whisper sweet nothings to the wild horses that run about the island, but the specific nature of that something is hard for him to pin down.

Malkovich has the time of his life with that search for Chris’ last speck of humanity, which shines up from the bottom of his soul as his mind continues to erode. At once both insidiously relaxed and also choked with Catholic guilt, Malkovich’s performance marries the nonchalance of a cowboy to the paranoia of a bounty target. One minute he’s waxing poetic about dinosaurs, and the next he’s rigging his luggage with explosives (maybe) and checking the “Memento”-like reminder notes he’s slipped into his jacket pocket.

“Wild Horse Nine” loves Chris too much to pretend like we’re not supposed to, but Malkovich never asks for our sympathy because he knows that he’ll get it anyway, and not just because the purpose of Rockwell’s character is to ensure that we do. It’s Chris’ job to make rooting for the bad guys feel like the right choice. It’s the cornerstone of America’s post-war foreign policy.

So while Chris might be cut from the same cloth as John Wayne (to the extent that Monument Valley is revealed to be a place of great importance to him), his arc is aimed in the opposite direction of the one that Ethan Edwards traces across “The Searchers”; Chris is a major asshole this movie gradually puckers into a wayward hero, and while it’s all too easy to root for him to complete that transformation before time runs out, at no point does “Wild Horse Nine” sell us on the premise that it would mean anything in the end — even to him.

The movie, blessedly, isn’t Catholic enough to offer Chris a big moment of divine expiation; in lieu of building to a grand confession, he and Lee simply run afoul of their CIA higher-ups until their PTO turns into a matter of American national security. Guns are fired. Hostages are taken. The word “fuck” is used like a punctuation mark, and regrets are muttered into the wind long after there’s any way for them to matter.

It all gets a bit too busy and madcap as “Wild Horse Nine” — freighted with sadness during even its cheekiest bits, as is McDonagh’s way — scrambles to make up for the general listlessness of its first half. Never as funny as it is sardonic, and always reaching so hard to be more of both, the film’s most successful moments are mined from the ambient tension between memory and erasure.

Chris, we begin to suspect, would do anything to forget what he’s done, and his own mind is graciously willing to get him halfway there. The rest of the CIA will do anything it takes to make sure that Chris doesn’t share whatever it is that he still remembers. Surrounding them on all sides are statues that predated America by several hundred years, and will likely continue to watch over Rapa Nui long after our empire has been wiped away like a tear in the rain. In “Wild Horse Nine,” American interventionism is less effective as the set-up for some jokes than it is as their punchline.

“Wild Horse Nine” premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Searchlight Pictures will release it in theaters on Friday, November 6.

#3489. Black Doves Season 3: Renewal Status & Everything We Know

Warning! This article contains SPOILERS for Black Doves season 2.Netflix's spy thriller Black Doves only just ended its second season, but many viewers are likely already wondering if the story of Keira Knightley's Helen Webb will continue in season 3. There's already a lot of hype surrounding Black Doves season 3. That's partly due to the rave reviews for Black Doves season 2 and partly due to the very open-ended finale of Black Doves season 2.

Black Doves has been a critical and popular darling since it began, and there's still plenty of room to explore Helen's story, so season 3 should be a no-brainer. Despite its popularity and success, the fate of Black Doves season 3 is still undecided. There are, however, a few hopeful indications that Netflix is going to make the right decision and renew Black Doves for another outing.

At the time of writing, Netflix has not yet officially confirmed Black Doves season 3. That's not a very discouraging development, as streaming services typically take weeks or months to issue a series renewal. It is, however, a bit unusual for Black Doves specifically. Black Doves season 2 was confirmed even before the first season premiered back in December 2024. It seems season 3 didn't get the same early vote of confidence, and it's possible that Netflix wants to look at critical reception and viewership numbers before deciding whether to renew or cancel the series.

Keira Knightley's Helen Webb / Daisy Bradshaw takes on various personas and undercover aliases in Netflix's thrilling espionage series Black Doves.

It is worth noting that Netflix's official ending explainer for Black Doves season 2 does explore what's next for the Black Doves following this season's reveals (via Tudum). While that's nowhere near an official renewal, it is a promising sign that Netflix is willing to renew the show for a third season and is already trying to drum up intrigue for some new plot lines. For now, however, the fate of Black Doves season 3 is unconfirmed.

Unfortunately, even if Black Doves season 3 is confirmed soon, this delay may have some implications for when it could be released on Netflix. Black Doves season 2, despite being renewed before season 1 even began, took nearly two full years to premiere. Since production on season 3 hasn't even begun yet, it may take even longer than season 2 did. So much is still up in the air, but Black Doves season 3 may not arrive on Netflix until 2028 or potentially later, if it happens at all.

Though the show hasn't been officially renewed yet, Black Doves showrunner Joe Barton has already hinted that he has plans for a third season. In an interview with Esquire, Barton said that he wants to have Tom Hanks and Elliot Page guest star in Black Doves season 3. While it's not exactly a confirmation that the script has been written, Barton's comments indicate that he at least has some idea of the story Black Doves season 3 could take.

Additionally, Barton also hinted at Helen's future during his interview with Netflix (via Tudum). In that interview, Barton mentions that Helen will likely go through an "evolution" as a character, and that her only path forward is to get even more involved in the Black Doves organization. Clearly, Barton has ideas about how to continue the story of Black Doves, even though Netflix hasn't given the official order yet.

One of the strongest pieces of evidence suggesting that Black Doves could be renewed for a third season is the ending of the second season. The finale of Black Doves season 2 left the door wide open for another season to pick up where it left off. It is by no means a definitive ending to Helen's story or the tale of the Black Doves as an organization; on the contrary, it actually seems Black Doves season 2 is an expansion of the show.

The clearest way Black Doves season 2 has expanded the series is through Kestrel, the new anarchist covert organization that stands opposed to the Black Doves. Though Katia, aka Vita, died at the end of season 2, Patrick was able to escape alive. He even delivered a calling card to Helen, which Reed smartly deduced was a warning that Kestrel had not been destroyed and could still pose a major threat. Reed also explained that Patrick had been seen boarding a plane to Tokyo, presumably to resume Kestrel's operations in the wake of Vita's death.

Kestrel presents a perfect story for Black Doves season 3 to explore. The next season could follow Helen and Reed tracking down Kestrel and trying to thwart their future actions across the globe. Kestrel also presents an opportunity to get government intelligence organizations, like the CIA and MI6, involved, as the U.S. and U.K. likely want revenge for Kestrel's attack on the peace summit. In short, Black Doves has set itself up very nicely to continue its story in season 3, even if that third season hasn't yet been confirmed.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3487. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.
