#3485. ‘The Weed Eaters’ Lands Expanded Release from Yellow Veil Pictures: New Zealand Cannibal Movie Sets Winter Rollout

Yellow Veil Pictures has boarded North American distribution rights for Callum Devlin‘s “The Weed Eaters,” a New Zealand cannibal horror film that notched a best feature win at SXSW Sydney in 2025. The indie banner is planning a winter release.

The deal for “The Weed Eaters” comes after the independent feature first debuted in the Unreleased Gems section of the Letterboxd Video Store, a video-on-demand streaming platform launched by the film-focused social media platform in 2025.

“Yellow Veil are consistently putting out the richest cinematic meals on offer, so it’s a real honour for ‘The Weed Eaters’ to be a part of their roster,” director Devlin wrote in a statement included in the deal’s announcement. “We always knew there was a global audience for this movie. I mean, this film is pretty gross. But the people that are into it are super into it, and we’re more than happy to make movies for the stoner freaks of the world.” Related Stories Inside Letterboxd’s Unlikely Distribution Pipeline: How ‘It Ends’ and Other Gems Found Their Way to a Deal Letterboxd Sale Talks Are Heating Up

“‘The Weed Eaters’ exemplifies what we have come to expect from New Zealand indie films. It’s filled with heart and humor, but this one’s not afraid to get weird and gross along the way,” reads a statement from Yellow Veil.

Exact details on the release plan for “The Weed Eaters” went undisclosed, though Yellow Veil is primarily a digital distribution company with ventures into limited theatrical play.

“The Weed Eaters” follows four friends that have their holiday getaway upended when they stumble upon a strain of marijuana that makes tokers crave the taste of human flesh. The film comes from Sports Team, Horse Bite, and Causeway Films, the Australian banner that was also behind titles like “The Babadook,” “Leviticus,” and “Bring Her Back.”

Prior to “The Weed Eaters,” several other titles featured on the Unreleased Gems section of the Letterboxd Video Store have gone on to land wider distribution, with one of the best-known examples being Neon’s acquisition of the cerebral horror film “It Ends.”

“We would never presume whether these filmmakers want to have a traditional distribution,” Letterboxd’s head of Video Store content Courtney Mayhew told IndieWire in August. “Even if it’s just five really strong ambassadors for these independent gems who will sing their praises and push for it and tell their friends about it … that’s something that has value.”

If Chris Pratt fans can't get enough of The Terminal List's military operations gone wrong, off-the-books missions, and powerful people secretly pulling the strings, Paramount+'s Lioness is your next watch. Created by Taylor Sheridan, Lioness exposes the darker side of serving one's country, where those on the front lines can be blindsided by greater interests that put not only their lives at risk but also the people around them.

Instead of a Navy SEAL commander, Lioness stars Zoe Saldaña as senior CIA case officer Joe McNamara, who also leads the covert Lioness program. Based on a real CIA initiative, the Lioness program sends female operatives to infiltrate the inner circles of designated targets by getting close to the women surrounding them. With the latest season of Lioness officially racking up an impressive 3.9 billion minutes viewed within just eight weeks, there's all the more reason for The Terminal List fans to check out the series.

In the aftermath of a failed Lioness mission in ISIS-controlled Syria that leaves her undercover operative dead, Joe (Saldaña) faces scrutiny from the CIA for taking drastic measures that nearly expose their involvement. Tasked with finding a replacement, she settles on Cruz Manuelos (Laysla De Oliveira), a Force Recon Marine turned Lioness operative assigned to get close to the daughter of an Iranian terrorist financier.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

Over the seasons, Lioness follows the tense working relationship between Joe and Cruz, with the former putting the latter through hell and back to prepare her for the assignment. But Cruz isn't the only operative to join the Lioness program. Season 2 introduces Captain Josephina Carrillo (Genesis Rodriguez), who's assigned to infiltrate a cartel. However, Season 3 takes a different turn from the usual Lioness formula, with Joe herself getting caught in direct danger and having to hope that the CIA reaches her in time before the worst happens.

Lioness isn't afraid to get its hands dirty. In The Terminal List Season 1, Reece's world falls apart after his platoon is ambushed during a mission and his wife and daughter are murdered in a separate attack. Driven by grief and a thirst for revenge, he compiles a target list of everyone responsible and sets out to kill them. As for Lioness, Joe doesn't have any personal vendettas, but the loss of her previous Lioness operative, partly due to her failure to properly vet them, and the mission's ultimate failure motivate her to hit back twice as hard. She needs someone willing to endure the program's downright problematic and highly triggering training methods, but Joe also has no qualms about sacrificing the operative herself if things go south.

However, despite Joe's seemingly cold-shouldered attitude toward her agents, which reflects the objective, no-mercy nature of CIA work, she is also a family woman. With a husband and children of her own, running a covert CIA program that the government refuses to acknowledge means her family has little protection if things go wrong. Given how many enemies Joe has made throughout her career, it's only a matter of time before her family, who already disapprove of her CIA work, becomes a target. And even Joe can't guarantee that she'll always be able to protect them.

It turns out that Kayce can't fully forget his past, after all.

While much of The Terminal List Season 1 follows Reece's personal quest for vengeance, Season 2 sees Reece pulled back by the CIA to stop a resurgent Al-Qaeda network. The same goes for Lioness, which follows Joe and her team as they conduct counterterrorism operations both inside and outside American borders. Joe believes her work is meant to protect innocent people from potential threats. However, both shows also question how much control these operatives actually have when their missions are linked to larger agendas.

If these thriller shows have shown anything, it's that politics and business often go hand in hand. Just as Reece discovers a conspiracy involving people who put his team in danger for their own financial gain, Joe learns in Lioness that terrorism isn't always an isolated threat. Behind these attacks are wealthy third parties who use terrorist groups to manipulate global economics and advance their own interests. With so much at stake, Lioness expands on what The Terminal List also explores — how national security can become a game played by people with too much power, leaving the soldiers on the ground the ones who must risk their lives to deal with the consequences.

Special Ops: Lioness is a Paramount+ original series starring Zoe Saldana and Nicole Kidman. The series centers on a marine and a CIA agent who work together with the daughter of a dangerous terrorist group to destroy the organization. Taylor Sheridan (Yellowstone co-creator) and Jill Wagner created the series, which was directed by Paul Cameron and Anthony Byrne.

#3481. Freida McFadden's 'The Housemaid' Stage Adaptation Announced

Freida McFadden has had no shortage of success, but 2026 has been especially fruitful for her.

The mystery author released a staggering four new books, all New York Times Bestsellers (The Witch, on October 6, The Divorce, on May 26, The Dinner Party on April 4, and Dear Debbie, on January 27). The Housemaid—the first film adaptation of McFadden's work—made over $400 million at the box office upon its December 2025 release, then became an even bigger streaming hit.

At least six more adaptations of her novels are now in development, including a sequel to The Housemaid, film versions of The Teacher, The Tenant, The Surrogate Mother, and The Divorce, and a series adaptation of Dear Debbie. The last year has been so big for McFadden that she even revealed the true identity behind her pen name after 12 years of keeping it a secret.

Now, however, the queen of mystery thrillers is venturing into even newer territory: one of her bestselling novels is coming to London as a play.

The Housemaid, a stage adaptation of McFadden’s 2022 novel, will premiere as a touring production in 2027, starting at Richmond Theatre in London.

Lionsgate, the studio behind the Housemaid films, will also produce this stage version. Playwright Bekah Brunstetter will write the script, while prolific West End director Matthew Dunster will direct. Both have experience developing major page-to-screen adaptations into stage productions: Brunstetter was Tony-nominated for her musical adaptation of Nicholas Sparks’ The Notebook, while Dunster recently directed The Hunger Games: On Stage.

While a straight play may not be the most expected avenue for adapting McFadden’s hit novels, mystery authors have a rich history with English theater. Agatha Christie wrote more than 15 plays during her life, including several adaptations of her own novels. One of her plays, The Mousetrap, has run consistently on the West End since 1952, making it the longest-running play in the world.

Sir Arthur Conan Doyle wrote 12 plays, including an adaptation of his Sherlock Holmes novels, and all premiered in England, while Dorothy L. Sayers wrote nine.

Set on Long Island, The Housemaid follows Millie Calloway, a young woman with a dark past who accepts a job as a live-in maid for a wealthy family, only to discover they have much darker secrets of their own.

The film adaptation stars Sydney Sweeney as Millie, with Amanda Seyfried and Brandon Sklenar as Nina and Andrew Winchester, the couple who employ her. A cast for the stage adaptation has yet to be announced, though it will follow the same general storyline.

The Housemaid will run for eight days at Richmond Theatre, starting September 11, 2027, and closing September 18—but tickets will be on sale as early as Friday, November 6. Future tour dates and locations are yet to be announced.

#3479. ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Denver Film Festival Top Prize as More Regional Fests Boost Oscar Hopefuls

Regional film festivals matter to a movie’s more cosmic position in the awards season, even if it started somewhere like Venice, Toronto, Telluride, Cannes, or even Sundance. They generate excitement from real-world audiences (and often Oscar voters, as in Middleburg, Virginia), and they also help unspool headlines that keep films top of mind for those who follow the race.

The 49th Denver Film Festival, held in the hip, high-altitude Colorado city every year, just wrapped its annual event — which this year ran October 22 to November 1. Denver Film CEO Kevin Smith, artistic director Matthew Campbell, and their team brought out special guests including Carrie Coon, John Leguizamo, John Cho, D’Arcy Carden, Peter Gamble, Indya Moore, Hans Petter Moland, and more to receive prizes and be feted with special tributes. Several of these, including Coon for “The Liberation” and Leguizamo for “The Odyssey,” are in the awards mix. Overall, Denver showcased 130 films, including many awards season favorites. Related Stories ‘Wild Horse Nine’ Review: Martin McDonagh’s Prickly but Unconvincing CIA Satire Recasts ‘In Bruges’ as the Stuff of a Classic Western ‘Hen’ Review: A Cockeyed Comedy Sees Europe’s Migrant Crisis Through the Eyes of a Chicken

I served on the documentary jury this year and awarded the Maysles Brothers Award to one of the year’s most revered docs. We chose the nonfiction portrait of adolescence “Whispers in May,” winner of this year’s CPH:DOX and from Chinese filmmaker Dongnan Chen, which is still seeking distribution. Per our statement penned with Vanity Fair’s Chris Murphy and producer Justine Suzanne Jones as fellow jurors, it’s “a vivid and compassionate portrait of female friendship in the twilight of adolescence” and “formally daring and emotionally authentic.” Other films in the category included “Once Upon a Time in Harlem,” “Edward Said: Between Worlds,” “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” “Nuisance Bear,” and “SUMO: Spirit Weighs Nothing.”

Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra,” which just won the BFI London Film Festival audience award after winning that same prize at TIFF in September, won the Krzysztof Kieslowski Award for Best Feature Film. The Spanish epic about gay desire and Federico García Lorca is locked in for multiple Oscar nominations at this point, with its awards streak going back to Best Director at Cannes in May.

The Audience Award for narrative feature, just as it did at the Virginia Film Festival in October, went to Peter Farrelly’s Sly Stallone behind-the-scenes biopic “I Play Rocky.” The film, starring charming breakout Anthony Ippolito as the “Rocky” star/screenwriter, was the runner-up to “La Bola Negra” in Toronto’s audience award category. “I Play Rocky” is in select theaters Thursday ahead of a November 20 wide release, and its popularity as an audience favorite is proving hard to best at fests.

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3476. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3475. Mike Flanagan's Next Stephen King Adaptation Marks A Career First

Faith Roswell is a Senior Writer on Screen Rant's Classic TV team. Since earning her degree in Creative Writing over a decade ago, Faith has written articles on film and TV from a variety of different angles. Faith now combines her knowledge of psychology with her love of monster movies to give more insight into what makes the best ones.  You may have read her Screen Rant lists and features covering horror, sci-fi, and fantasy, or read her Amazon Top 10 book, "Movie Monsters of the Deep." Faith has had an extensive career as a writer, appearing on BBC live radio, researching true crime for Rotten Mango podcast, and writing for publications including Mental Floss, Atlas Obscura, and The Daily Jaws before beginning here at Screen Rant.

Mike Flanagan's chain of horror successes has cemented his status as one of the best filmmakers of the past few decades, with his ability to adapt Stephen King's work changing the game for both. Stephen King and Mike Flanagan's collaborations have been some of the greatest recent movies and TV shows in the horror genre, with the success of the Carrie TV adaptation laying the groundwork for much more ambitious projects. One of these is set to be a career first for Flanagan, not only due to its immense scale, but because of its genre change.

Stephen King's works have often been difficult to adapt, but this is where Mike Flanagan has shone, with a talent for screening the "unadaptable." With the filmmaker owning the rights to The Dark Tower, he has made no secret of the fact that he wants to make a TV version of the novel series after the movie adaptation failed disastrously, famously telling Empire Magazine that "we can’t let that [movie] be the final word. We really can’t." Still, the novel series is a complex mix of genres that is almost certain to give the horror filmmaker a creative challenge.

While Carrie is connected to Stephen King's wider mythology, with its confirmed second season set to explore his universe in greater detail, most of Mike Flanagan's best TV shows and movies have been on a relatively small scale. This has led many to wonder if The Dark Tower's epic scale will be too ambitious. Forming the center of the entire Stephen King universe, the story spans seven main novels and a novella, and takes place within a multiverse in which time is not always linear, allowing for some meta twists.

Flanagan appears to be growing in confidence, with his upcoming Warhammer 40,000 series being a drastic departure from shows like The Haunting of Hill House and Midnight Mass, which are self-contained masterpieces but do not touch the level of complexity and lore that The Dark Tower will need. Still, another factor is likely to challenge him more than the novel series' scale, and that is its genre. The Dark Tower crosses Stephen King with Tolkien and a classic Western, with characters like The Gunslinger embarking on epic quests in mysterious lands full of strange creatures.

The Dark Tower lore crosses over into Stephen King's other works, with characters appearing in The Stand, Salem's Lot, and several other books.

Flanagan's shows are generally atmospheric and aesthetic, but they have a much more grounded tone than The Dark Tower, as King's fantasy writing can verge on the absurd. Despite delivering perfect TV shows involving demons and hauntings, The Dark Tower's wizards, talking animals and increasingly bizarre characters are an entirely different theme for Flanagan to tackle. Still, after delivering the news that Stephen King fans were waiting for, explaining that the books will be adapted in order, this removes one main challenge with adapting The Dark Tower, but whether Flanagan can convey its fantasy tone remains to be seen.

Of all the terrible book to movie adaptations, The Dark Tower is one of the most infamous. Despite its beloved source material and the presence of both Idris Elba and Matthew McConaughey, The Dark Tower has just a 16% positive score on Rotten Tomatoes, with both critics and audiences agreeing that it went wrong in virtually every way possible. Rather than starting on a small scale and expanding the story, the movie attempted to fit the entire novel series into just 95 minutes, resulting in a shallow and confusing disaster.

King's book series begins with the words "The man in black fled across the desert, and the gunslinger followed," instantly establishing a classic Western tone, while other genres like fantasy and horror emerge as the story continues. The movie failed to capture this genre blend, instead turning the epic tale into a PG-13 action movie with a revenge plot. However, with Flanagan confirming that he intends to build the story slowly, he will have time to capture its unique tone, and it will not be the first time that he has crossed genres.

Flanagan might be best known for horror, but his projects feature elements of other genres. Carrie captures an authentic high school atmosphere, selling the psychological drama before the iconic prom scene. His King adaptation, The Life of Chuck, leans into whimsy and fantasy, and Doctor Sleep introduces a dark fantasy tone that already proves he can blend genres. These might be minor when compared to the extensive lore of The Dark Tower, but Flanagan is ready for this career first, and with even its author calling him "the King whisperer," he is the perfect director to do the story justice.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#3474. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3473. ‘Everytime’ Review: Sandra Wollner’s Infinitely Beguiling Portrait of Grief in the Digital Age Is One of the Most Haunting Films of the Decade

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 10, 2026 during the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release the film in limited theaters Friday, November 6, with a wide release to come in February 2027.]

I don’t believe in an afterlife, but that’s OK because the people I love most are never going to die. Not to me. At least, not in the way they used to before our species began to migrate online, to store our memories in the cloud, and to digitally encode the raw data of our existence onto everything we touch.

My father was born in 1939, the same year that Iowa State College scientists John Vincent Atanasoff and Clifford Berry built the prototype for the first binary-based computer; in the months after he died 75 years later, I often felt the reflex to reach down and call him from the iPhone that fit inside my pocket. To ask if he’d seen the Rangers game, or to tell him that I’d gotten engaged. I knew that he was gone, of course, but the piece of consumer technology I’d used to connect with him when he was alive had created a separate neural pathway between my brain and his being — a crude one-way network that didn’t begin to break down until much later in my grieving process.  Related Stories I Remember ‘Rocky’: My Front Row Seat to the Marketing of a Million-to-One Blockbuster MUBI Has Cleared the Path for Sandra Hüller to Land Multiple Oscar Nominations This Season

A decade later, those pathways have grown exponentially more complicated and convincing. The emergence of AI has led to a variety of ghoulish attempts at deathlessness and resurrection (from bots that feed on your grandma’s Facebook data to the ChatGPT Theodore Roosevelt who Trump was “honored to be with today” at the former’s Presidential Library), but such products and publicity stunts miss the fact that everyone is already being (temporarily) immortalized on a server farm somewhere, the traces of our existence shed into the digital ether like a Pollock-like splotch of invisible ink.

Charlie Kirk’s face is Twitter’s most ubiquitous meme. My long-deceased college friend you’ve never heard of sends me hacked emails full of links to “old pictures they found of us together.” The cancer-stricken hedgehog I fostered for a few months in 2016 still cycles onto my home screen at random sometimes, and he’s now been buried behind a house in suburban New Jersey for longer than he was ever alive. People have always looked for errant glimmers of the dead in the world around them, but now the past runs parallel to — imprints upon, and circles around — the present to a degree that can severely confuse the relationship between the two.

Sandra Wollner doesn’t believe in an afterlife either, but she’s certainly attuned to the mysteries of this one. Picking up where the equally spectral likes of “Personal Shopper” and “Aftersun” left up, the Austrian writer/director’s mystical and magnificently beguiling “Everytime” takes a rather ambivalent stance towards what happens when people die these days, or at least — per its curious title — towards how we mourn them from inside the flat circle of a temporal overlap where yesterday and tomorrow are folded into the pockets of an ever-expanding now.

There are no clear answers to be found in this astonishing third feature, which shares a number of thematic similarities with Wollner’s “The Trouble with Being Born,” but retains one crucial difference (that film, about a man who has an implied sexual relationship with a child-sized android coded with the memories of his missing 10-year-old daughter, unsurprisingly had trouble securing American distribution). Indeed, the grounded portraiture of the movie’s first 70 minutes eventually gives way to a final act so cosmic and surreal that it becomes all but impossible to pinpoint the precise location of Wollner’s characters in space-time; to say for certain whether “Everytime” has glitched into another dimension, or if it has invited another dimension to glitch into our own. Initially timeless in its nuanced and deeply recognizable depiction of loss, and then even more so as it gets devoured by the meta-modern flourishes that have fringed its story from the start, this is perhaps the most forward-thinking film I’ve ever seen about the changing face of grief.

The premise couldn’t be simpler, though Wollner’s incredible prologue — a careful arrangement of low-event long takes that emphasize how people move through spaces in time — trains our eyes to privilege texture over incident. While there’s little to distinguish single mother Ella (“Everyone Else” star Brigit Minichmayr) and her children from any of the other families strolling through the soft orange haze of a summer afternoon in Berlin, our senses pick up on the uneasy tension between the watchfulness of Gregory Oke’s 35mm camera work and the vivid intensity of the film’s sound design (it’s worth noting that Oke also shot “Aftersun”). The voices are close, but the bodies far away. Teenage Jessie (Carla Hüttermann) turns her head to look at an unseen pop as her family walks home through their local metro station, but we don’t think much of it at the moment. It’s probably nothing. And yet, I suppose it could be anything.

At the very least, that sharp noise is enough to suggest that the film’s environments may not be as benign as they seem, and a silent but soon unbearable tension starts to mount as the day wears on. As Jessie’s boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) comes over to hang out while her kid sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling) annoys the shit out of her by banging on a keyboard; as Ella cooks dinner; as Jessie plays “Minecraft” late into the night on an island bathed in the light of a sinking square sun.

Later, in the waning hours before Jessie’s family is due to leave for a holiday in Tenerife (where she once vacationed as a toddler), Jessie and Lux will sneak out to a dance club, take a few pills, and watch the next day begin from their perch atop the roof of an apartment building. He will note that he’s recently noticed a strange number of seagulls in Berlin, and then fall asleep. She will stand up to film one of them flying past on her iPhone, and then — in one of the most arresting screen images in recent memory, a vertiginous collision of everything and nothing all at once — she will fall off the edge of the building to her death. The city doesn’t notice. The camera scans the treetops. The euphoric synth-pop of David Schweighart’s score kicks in as we suddenly begin to soar through the skies of Jessie’s “Minecraft” world, eventually plunging down through the dirt and into the unrendered levels of code below.

From there, “Everytime” settles into a crushingly quotidian register. Months have passed, and everyone is doing what they can to move on with their lives. Ella takes work calls while visiting her daughter’s grave, while the stoic young Melli texts life updates and other messages to her dead sister’s phone (she’s big on emojis). But things are not as settled as they seem, and Lux’s return from a semester abroad forces Ella and Melli into a more direct confrontation with Jessie’s memory — with the unresolved feelings she left behind. The girls keep running into Lux (and to his nice new girlfriend) around town, and soon begin spending time with him on purpose. They are bound together not only by their shared grief, but also by the unspoken guilt and blame that Lux and Ella can only hope to expiate through each other.

While Jessie is seldom mentioned by name, the bizarre mutual reliance between a middle-aged woman and her dead teenage daughter’s former boyfriend makes her the subject of every scene (much to the annoyance of people who would prefer to compartmentalize the pain of her loss). Jessie is the reason why Ella and Melli attend Lux’s birthday party; Jessie is the reason why Lux joins Ella for a tense lunch at her ex-husband’s house, and why he begins sleeping over at her apartment.

But these domestic frictions are — largely, but not merely — a means to an end so far as Wollner is concerned, as her film leverages them to focus on a series of increasingly abstract phenomena. Jessie is certainly the reason why each of the locations we saw her walk through before her death feels haunted when “Everytime” revisits them, but could she also be the reason why the shadow that falls across her bedroom at night appears to resemble a polygonal cube? Why a seemingly pilotless drone shows up to beckon Ella into a pitch-black parking garage? Why the dead girl’s computer glows with an unnatural brightness whenever the lights turn off?

Wollner’s characters never ask such questions aloud, but she poses them to all three of her leads in a way that compels them to look for signs in the digital detritus that Jessie left behind. Lux is drawn back to the old pictures and voice notes on his phone, while Mille stares at the WhatsApp chat with her sister as if waiting for a response. These signs complement, but never overwhelm, Wollner’s attention to the analog poetry of the natural world — to the shimmer along the surface of a lake, or the sound of the wind rustling through the trees in the woods where Jessie and Lux got high on her last night.

It’s easy to imagine a version of this film that more explicitly addressed how digital technology is transforming how we mourn the dead, but Wollner would rather plumb the mysteries of the present than speculate about the answers of the future; the portals between worlds have already been ripped open, and will only begin to lose their power as they get labeled and branded.

Eventually, Ella makes the spontaneous decision to bring Mille and Lux to Tenerife for the trip they never got to take. That’s where things get weird, and the math of the universe starts to contradict itself. It would be a terrible disservice to reveal anything specific about what happens next (and so I won’t), but the extraordinary magic trick that “Everytime” pulls off in its final stretch is rooted less in incident than in execution.

Its ineffable power belongs to how matter-of-factly Wollner tears apart the fabric of her film’s reality at the same time as she threads it together, and how the look on Minichmayr’s slacken face — her restrained but masterful performance a wonder of tightly bottled pain and lingering disbelief — reconciles those opposite energies with the instinctive naturalness of a mother’s love. It also belongs to the almost unquestioning acceptance that Keiling endows within Melli, the young actor’s posture embodying how this movie teeters on the precipice between a child-like vision of the world (soft and malleable) and the more hardened sense of reality that arrives with adulthood.

Wollner may not trace the character’s arc in the legible terms of a typical coming-of-age story, but Melli experiences a remarkable transformation over the course of the film, her petulant first line (“You always leave your stuff lying around!”) assuming an unforeseeable new context by the time we arrive at her closing narration.

As a medium born from — and once dependent upon smoothing over — the friction between stillness and movement, stasis and change, cinema has always been uniquely adept at conveying the radical effect that technology can exert on how we perceive time and space in the world around us. The switch from celluloid to computer chips saw the movies transform from an illusory art form to a representative one, at the great and continued risk of forfeiting its original power. Engaging in a thrilling and increasingly contested negotiation between 35mm film stock and crude DV video formats, “Everytime” pulls at that tug-of-war from both ends until the uncertain space at the center grows large enough to sail through, and still enough to hang like a painting in the sky.

I am now a father myself, the parent of two young kids whose faces sometimes remind me of my own dad in the same tactile way that people have been survived by their children since before the invention of the wheel. We keep a framed 4×6 photograph of him with a cigar in his mouth on the Blu-ray shelf in our living room, and I sometimes catch my kids talking about it as if the picture itself were their grandfather, rather than just a capture of his likeness. Ask my six-year-old to draw a self-portrait and he’ll sketch you the image of his Roblox avatar. If I ever were to lose him, I wonder how long it would take my nervous system to process that he was gone.

Like many 21st century parents, my wife and I take photos and videos of our kids throughout the day without thinking, and — after wrestling them to bed at night in an exasperating forever war of attrition — we invariably scroll through our phones and take stock of their cuteness in peace. Stills, videos, stickers, and more, these two-dimensional images, I sometimes feel with an uncertain pang of dismay, are our real children. The versions of them we commit to memory. The after images we see in our dreams. They are the kids we mourn as our son and daughter eagerly outgrow their current models every time you look away for too long, and the ones we would cling to in the unthinkable event that either of them disappeared from this mortal coil before we did.

And so, Wollner’s staggering new film suggests with a tender but uneasy twinkle in its eye, we’ve gradually steeped ourselves in a world that guarantees they never will. How strange and unnatural is that? Compared to the alternative, I fear it may not feel that strange or unnatural at all.

“Everytime” is screening at the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. 1-2 Special will release it in theaters in the United States.

#3471. 6 Forgotten Movie Trilogies Where Every Movie Is 10/10, No Notes

Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Plenty of trilogies run on a single continuous storyline that carries through from start to finish. Then there are the trios that keep looping back to the same central theme, location, or human struggle from entirely different angles. That second group hits differently because each entry works as a standalone piece while still retroactively reshaping how every character decision feels.

In fact, these six selections show just how far that thematic approach can stretch. The entries range from awkward Swedish salesmen trying to hawk plastic vampire teeth to a massive nine-and-a-half-hour epic about surviving war with your soul intact. Every single title here earns its keep without needing the surrounding films to lean on. Plot twist, together they hit harder.

Roy Andersson’s The Living trilogy includes Songs from the Second Floor, You, the Living, and A Pigeon Sat on a Branch Reflecting on Existence. The trilogy has no continuing plot. Instead, it keeps returning to ordinary people facing humiliation, grief, and the daily effort to carry on.

In Songs, Kalle (Lars Nordh) burns down his failing business for insurance money, then tries selling wooden crosses at a trade fair. You gives a teacher breaking down in class while a military band plays. Pigeon follows Sam (Nils Westblom) and Jonathan (Holger Andersson), two salesmen who cannot sell their vampire teeth. Laughter quickly turns into discomfort as the camera holds on them after another failed pitch. Every carefully staged scene makes embarrassment feel painfully human. That's the real genius here, because the trilogy forces viewers to pay closer attention to people having a terrible day.

The Proletariat trilogy was never planned as a three-part project from the start. Instead, these three films gradually came together to form a raw portrait of working people trying to secure some tenderness and control over their lives. Shadows in Paradise pairs garbage collector Nikander (Matti Pellonpää) with supermarket cashier Ilona (Kati Outinen). Their romance keeps running into disappointments and awkward practical problems.

In Ariel, Taisto’s (Turo Pajala) father gives him a Cadillac, then kills himself. Taisto is robbed, jailed, escapes, and tries to leave Finland with Irmeli (Susanna Haavisto) and her son. The Match Factory Girl follows Iris (Kati Outinen) from a factory line to a home where her parents ignore her. After a date treats her as disposable, she buys rat poison. That turn is brutal, inspiring a protective feeling for Iris even as she commits terrible acts. Still, the signature deadpan humor never makes her humiliation the joke.

Labeling Bill Douglas’s trilogy as merely bleak leaves out the heart of the story. My Childhood follows eight-year-old Jamie (Stephen Archibald) in a Scottish mining village, with his mother institutionalized and his father absent. His brother Tommy (Hughie Restorick) is one of the few people who shares his daily life.

In My Ain Folk, Jamie is sent to live with his paternal grandmother. His grandfather gives him affection, and losing him leaves Jamie with little comfort at home. My Way Home takes Jamie through foster care, a homeless shelter, and the RAF. In Egypt, he meets Robert (Joseph Blatchley), whose friendship gives him kindness without asking him to earn it first. Stephen Archibald lets viewers watch Jamie grow without making him a symbol of suffering. It feels infuriating that kindness took so long to find him. Yet the moment it does, the gratitude is overwhelming.

Where Is the Friend’s House? gives Ahmad (Babak Ahmadpour) a simple, urgent problem. He has his classmate’s notebook, and the boy may be punished if Ahmad does not return it. Ahmad walks from village to village, asking for help. You are rooted for him the entire time. The notebook matters because he understands what the punishment will mean to his friend.

And Life Goes On sends a father and son through earthquake-damaged roads, searching for the child actors from the first film. Through the Olive Trees follows a crew making that second film, while actor Hossein (Hossein Rezai) keeps trying to court Tahereh (Tahereh Ladanian), who refuses him outside their scenes together. These aren’t plot sequels so much as films that keep revisiting a village and the people living there. It is amazing how much care goes into everything, from a massive natural disaster right down to two actors sitting in uncomfortable silence.

Instead of a standard sequence of stories, BRD acts as a sharp portrait of female survival, showing three distinct bargains available to women in a society eager to prosper and forget. In The Marriage of Maria Braun, Maria (Hanna Schygulla) uses ambition and beauty to build security during the economic recovery after her husband disappears. Lola shifts the dynamic, following a cabaret singer-prostitute (Barbara Sukowa) who calculates every move, maneuvering around a corrupt contractor and a new building commissioner for money, property, and love. Sukowa’s confidence in the role is a total pleasure to watch.

Then Veronika Voss drops into complete obscurity, tracking a former Nazi-era film star (Rosel Zech) trapped by her need for help and dependent on a doctor, while sportswriter Robert Krohn (Hilmar Thate) looks into her decline. What stays with you is how differently these three films approach the exact same struggle. Maria negotiates, Lola calculates, and Veronika succumbs. Together, their choices expose the precise price tag postwar West Germany placed on getting ahead.

Across nine and a half grueling hours, this trilogy tracks a single man’s moral destruction as every attempt to act decently backfires. Kaji (Tatsuya Nakadai) starts in No Greater Love taking a job supervising forced Chinese labor in Manchuria to avoid conscription, trying to improve the workers’ conditions. That decency gets him beaten, costs him his exemption, and drags him directly into the Imperial Army. In Road to Eternity, the military's relentless demand for obedience costs him people he respects.

By A Soldier’s Prayer, he is left a prisoner walking through snow toward his wife Michiko (Michiyo Aratama) until he dies. The tragedy is that Kaji’s best intentions constantly end up hurting the people he wants to protect. Kaji is never presented as flawless, which only makes his downward spiral feel more agonizing. Truth is, the desperate hope for him to just make it home haunts you long after the credits roll. It hits like a brick.

#3470. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.

Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.

Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.

Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3468. Two ‘Ramayana’ Cuts Are in Theaters — but Your Best Bet for the Indian Epic Is Clear

“Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” retells a millennia-old Hindu epic on a splashy scale. The Hindi-language studio film — part one of a planned duology — has been released outside India by Sony Pictures, which hopes to make it a cross-cultural hit by courting audiences who don’t normally spend every weekend watching the latest Bollywood fare. Among the strategies for this rollout have been a lavish Comic-Con panel, as well as an English dub of the movie, which was the version shown to press prior to the review embargo. However, language isn’t the only difference; this version is almost half an hour shorter than the Hindi original and excises some make-or-break material. Related Stories ‘Everytime’ Review: Sandra Wollner’s Infinitely Beguiling Portrait of Grief in the Digital Age Is One of the Most Haunting Films of the Decade ‘La Bola Negra’ Wins Denver Film Festival Top Prize as More Regional Fests Boost Oscar Hopefuls

The Hindi version did eventually screen for press (about a day before the film’s release), but by then, early reviews quickly noted the awkward method of its transposition. Dubbing into different languages is hardly new, but AI-assisted lip syncing to match the actors’ mouth movements gives the English performances a stilted quality. Granted, the in-house program developed for this purpose (named “Brahma AI” after the Hindu creator-god, who features in one of the movie’s many prologues) seems a tad more ethical than most generative AI. The process involves real human beings recording the English lines — in some cases, the original actors themselves — as well as real mouth performances (creepy as that sounds) captured to map onto the original faces. Essentially, its data sets seem to be entirely internal, so the stealing aspect of the wider AI problem isn’t a concern here. However, the effect is distracting by way of exaggerated lip movements, and the English dialogue itself is clunky and emotionally restricting.

This becomes all too clear when watching the Hindi version for comparison, which I managed to on opening day at New York’s Mecca for Indian movies: the labyrinthine, 25-screen AMC in Times Square. The original cut doesn’t make the movie magically great — it still has the same haphazard approach to building action, and the same uncanny CGI — but it does call into question the methods by which Sony has attempted to localize (and globalize) the film for wider viewership. Most obviously: performances are more emotionally convincing in their original form, and the reverb on the original dialogue is much more befitting of a large-scale epic, while the mixing for the English lines conjures images of a claustrophobic studio booth. However, the more baffling comparison is between the different cuts, and how each one affects the story.

The English cut runs 166 minutes, which is about half an hour shorter than the original. With that much of a lag, you’d expect the discrepancies to be obvious early on, but surprisingly, the two films are mostly identical for about the first two hours. They cover largely the same ground, between the origins of the demon king Ravana (Yash), the condensed upbringing of the heroic prince Rama (Ranbir Kapoor), and his eventual exile to the forest alongside his graceful wife Sita (Sai Pallavi) and his devoted brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey). The differences are largely in how scenes play out, especially montages backed by songs.

The film has few traditional dance numbers, but in sequences where wider details from the poem are squeezed into the running time, the English version snips them here and there, removing only minor subplots at first. For instance, when Rama and Sita meet and talk for the first time, Rama’s three brothers can also be seen flirting with various women around the palace, as the prince mentions only wanting to marry Sita if his siblings can be married on the same day. This is absent in the English version, as are shots of the additional three weddings during Rama and Sita’s ceremony. It’s not the most vital thing to include from a plot standpoint, though it arguably gestures toward the nature of the story at large, as one in which Rama tries to stick to his promises, as fate contorts itself in his favor.

Still, this and some other deletions aren’t necessarily missed for much of the running time, like a few extra action beats in existing scenes, and additional shots of Rama and Sita living in their kingdom, Ayodhya, and getting to know its people, in another musical montage. However, they give the story a bit of breathing room, which is never a bad thing. In any case, the most destructive removal is far more noticeable. It arrives about two hours into the Hindi running time, by way of a single dramatic scene (or a trio of scenes in quick succession, depending on how you count them) that makes for the film’s emotional centerpiece, and practically resolves major issues with the English version’s latter half.

Both films conclude with the giant, humanoid bird king Jatayu trying to rescue Sita from a flying chariot when she’s kidnapped by Ravana, in a scene that, while visually dazzling, feels a tad random as the climax to its own movie (rather than a midpoint or inciting incident; the epic has been split quite inelegantly). This in turn leads to a mournful speech from Rama about rejecting his destiny and writing his own path as he plans to march on Ravana’s kingdom of Lanka. In the English cut, this feels like a distinction without a difference, since Rama’s training by various priests and sages has, in fact, been in anticipation of a conflict with Ravana. However, many of these dangling threads feel more emotionally whole in the Hindi version, thanks to the aforementioned scenes, known traditionally as the Bharat Milap, or the meeting with Bharat, Rama’s brother, who was placed on the throne in his stead.

In a subplot wholly absent from the English cut, a royal procession reaches Rama’s humble hut, where Bharat — who knew nothing of the palace conspiracy to replace Rama as king — informs him of their father’s death. In the English version, it’s never clear when, if ever, Rama learns about this major development (which even comes up in the film’s concluding scene), leaving viewers to intuit that it probably happened off screen. However, this isn’t even the only problem the Bharat Milap solves.

After Rama scatters his father’s ashes, the two brothers have an emotional conversation with Lakshmana by their side. Bharat tries to convince Rama to return to Ayodhya and take the throne, but Rama believes this ascetic path has been laid out for him as part of his fate and sacred duty, so he decides to remain in the forest. All the while, Lakshmana harbors a grudge against Bharat, and is angered by Rama’s decision to remain in exile, though he goes along with it as part of his own duty and moral code.

For one thing, this makes Lakshmana make a whole lot more sense as a character in subsequent scenes, in which he occasionally flies off the handle. Without these vital exchanges informing his state of mind, his volatility seems arbitrary (though sadly, neither version manages to make his comedic quips really land). For another, these missing scenes give Rama an actual character arc, and imbue the film with a vital throughline of how various characters approach the idea of divine destiny.

When Sita is kidnapped, and Rama comforts the dying Jatayu — who, by the way, features briefly in these missing scenes as well, making his climactic arrival less sudden — there’s a sense of direct causality to these events. Rama isn’t just a witness to his wife’s abduction and Jatayu’s slaying, but he feels the guilt of having made the decision to remain alone and vulnerable in the first place. When he talks of rejecting destiny and writing his own story, these cease to be the mere platitudes of the English version. They become a direct callback to his own decision-making, in which he chose to follow the lifelong path laid out before him, out of a sense of divine obligation.

This, in turn, affects another scene (albeit a smaller one) in which Ravana and his siblings bicker over whether to kidnap Sita in the first place. The notion of destiny comes up once more, in the idea that Ravana going down this violent path is something the gods might actually want to entrap him in a battle with Rama. Since the movie is a mere first half, its primary hero and villain never interact, and they don’t even feel thematically bound in the English version. In the original cut, these notions of destiny, as laid out by Rama’s chat with Bharat, set the protagonist and antagonist on an unavoidable collision course.

The decision to cut the running time makes roundabout sense, given that one of the few things most Western viewers know about Hindi movies is their historically enormous lengths. However, when Hollywood films like the “Avatar” sequels and “Avengers: Endgame” (and even Indian hits like the Telugu-language “RRR”) draw crowds with three-plus-hour running times, this phantom barrier clearly isn’t insurmountable. Shaving things down to a still-robust 2 hours and 46 minutes isn’t likely to be the deciding factor for many viewers; people tend to round up or down at that length.

While this feels akin to a Harvey Weinstein-esque interference, this particular decision was, according to Sony, made with the input of the team behind “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend.” But whatever the impetus for these competing cuts — both of which are now in theaters — the decision to cleave out such a vital emotional and thematic crux, the meeting between the brothers, is utterly confounding. It’s the story’s heart and soul, and erasing it is downright destructive to how the movie plays. So, if you’re deciding between the two versions, the choice should be pretty clear.

#3467. iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, and it reintroduces the all-new Health app that was first available for testing during the iOS 27.2 beta. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27.3 will launch with an upgraded Apple Health app. The new app was initially tested during the iOS 27.2 beta, but it’s back today in iOS 27.3 beta 1 and will ship to all users next month.

Today on Apple Newsroom, the company outlined what to expect from the new Health experience.

Three central new Health features are highlighted for iOS 27.3:

Insights tab: “surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.”

Longevity tab: “analyzes longitudinal metrics across heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement, metabolic health, hearing, and nutrition. Central to this tab is Health Age, a feature that translates data from Apple Watch — including VO2 max, resting heart rate, sleep, and heart rate variability — into a metric that reflects how a user’s body is tracking relative to their chronological age. Users can also incorporate clinical laboratory data, such as A1c and LDL cholesterol, to enrich their long-term health picture.”

At-home movement evaluations: “make physical assessments accessible without requiring specialized equipment. Using an iPhone camera and Apple Watch, users can measure their flexibility, strength, balance, movement mechanics, and VO2 max with real-time audio and visual feedback. Powered by on-device vision-based AI models and developed with clinical experts, the experience runs entirely on device; no video is ever recorded, stored, or shared.“

Additionally, Apple says that the new Health app offers expanded language support. It is available in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

#3466. Dungeons & Dragons’ New Species Is Officially Broken

A new playable species added to Dungeons and Dragons with the release of the World of Warcraft expansion is officially broken, and if you like taking to the skies with aasimar and aarakocra characters, you’re going to love this one. The release of D&D: World of Warcraft has added tons of character options, monsters, and much more from Blizzard’s iconic MMORPG to the TTRPG. Players can now control their favorite characters from Azeroth in a tabletop setting, and this expansion is quite complete, featuring things like classes, professions, and more.

By using the new subclasses in D&D: World of Warcraft, players can even play Death Knights, Demon Hunters, and Evokers at their tables. There are also new subclasses for classic classes, like the Oath of the Holy subclass for Paladins. In addition to all of that, players can choose new or reworked species. You can, for instance, play a Blood Elf, which is a lineage for the Elf in the 2024 Player’s Handbook, or pick an entirely new species, such as the Vulpera. In total, the expansion offers 16 species options, but one of them is delightfully broken.

Following the classes in D&D: World of Warcraft, there are species options, and the very first of them is already a perfect choice. The Dracthyr arrive in Dungeons and Dragons, and despite their visual similarities to the Dragonborn, they are very different, especially when it comes to rules. Dracthyr have Darkvision with a range of 60 feet, which feels standard, but there are many species that don’t have access to Darkvision. Dracthyr can also use their wings and tails as weapons with their Natural Weaponry trait, letting them make an Unarmed Strike to shove a creature as a Bonus Action.

However, Dracthyr have extra traits that make them even more special. Gliding Wings lets them subtract 100 feet from the distance fallen when calculating the fall’s damage, and they can move up to 2 feet horizontally for every 1 foot they descend. Mechanically speaking, you can fall up to 100 feet without ever taking damage, and up to 200 feet reducing the damage you take. It’s not as good as the damage-nullifying Glide trait from the Hadozee species in Dungeons and Dragons. However, Dracthyr also gain a ton of horizontal mobility, letting you reach far-away locations.

The Dracthyr from World of Warcraft, within the TTRPG setting, also have the Visage trait. This ability lets them use a Magic action to shape-shift into a humanoid form, called a visage, or back to their natural Dragon form. On top of how cool it is to technically design two different characters, a visage can come in handy in locations where a Dracthyr would feel out of place, or when trying to escape authorities. Last but not least, Dracthyr have the Draconic Flight trait, unlocked at level 5.

As a Bonus Action, you can leap into the air and gain a Fly Speed equal to your Speed for 10 minutes. This can only be used once per Long Rest. Flight is extremely powerful in the game, and while it isn’t as good as an aarakocra’s game-breaking level 1 flight, it is better than the aasimar’s flight. With it, you can fly around slinging spells or firing arrows in combat, or reach otherwise impossible locations. With the proper build to take advantage of these traits, Dracthyr are the most broken species in Dungeons and Dragons’ World of Warcraft expansion.
