#3416. L.A. District Attorney Nathan Hochman Rips Gavin Newsom For Commuting Death Sentences

Gavin Newsom is sparing hundreds of inmates from execution in California ... but Los Angeles County's top prosecutor says the governor can't wipe out the death penalty entirely.

In a statement Thursday, District Attorney Nathan Hochman acknowledged Newsom has the constitutional power to commute death sentences ... but stressed, "That power does not extend to eliminating the death penalty."

Hochman pointed out California voters have twice rejected efforts to eliminate the death penalty ... pointing out only voters or the state Legislature can change that law.

Hochman's not backing down ... saying his office will continue considering the death penalty in all eligible cases as long as it remains legal.

He also turned his attention to victims' families ... saying they deserve a justice system that honors the law and treats their cases fairly.

As TMZ previously reported ... Newsom announced plans Thursday to commute the sentences of all 548 California death row inmates to life in prison without parole, arguing state-sanctioned executions are incompatible with California's values.

But there's a catch ... hundreds of those commutations still need approval from the California Supreme Court, and the death penalty itself remains on the books.

#3415. Will Trump Bring Down His Pumped-Up God of War?

For more than a year and a half, Pete Hegseth has been one of Donald Trump’s most valuable Cabinet members.

He is muscular and energetic, fueled by a seemingly limitless drive to do some kind of crossfit maneuver with anyone who remains in his orbit for too long. And, like Trump, who once had his young son fast forward through the parts in Bloodsport that didn’t involve fighting, Hegseth loves violence. The man loves war so much that he renamed his job to have the word “war” in it, and then helped Trump launch one of the most ill-advised conflicts in recent memory. They learned this week that perhaps they like war a little bit more than the American public, who voted for basically every Democrat on their ballots in one of the worst midterm defeats for a ruling party in living memory. All this means that Trump now faces a choice: stand by his loyal Titan of Testosterone, or give Hegseth the axe.

The choice could be made for him, of course. Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, who was booted from the MAGA movement when Trump endorsed his primary opponent earlier this year, has said that he will trigger a vote to impeach Hegseth as soon as Congress returns to session next week. Even if Massie’s resolution passes the House, at least 67 senators would need to support removing him from his role, which means the most likely way Hegseth will leave the Pentagon is the president deciding it’s time for him to go.

So far, though, Trump has been somewhat even-handed. In an interview with ABC News on Thursday, Trump said he has “every intention to keep” Hegseth in his role. “I get these calls, you know, about him. I don’t understand why,” Trump said. Behind the scenes, though, Trump has also reportedly been asking advisers if they think he should give Hegseth the boot.

“Hegseth is on the chopping block,” one former White House staffer told Fox News.

Trump seems to be mulling this decision over in public. On Wednesday, he said that Hegseth was “doing a very good job” as Secretary of Defense, but also said that Hegseth would be “very popular” if he did choose to move into a different role in politics — such as, say, the Senate seat in Tennessee. Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn will be vacating her seat next year after winning the race to become governor of the state, raising the possibility that she could appoint Hegseth to serve out the rest of her term in the Senate. JD Vance, meanwhile, posted a lengthy post-midterms message blaming the GOP’s poor showing on the war.

Trump’s choice isn’t as simple as it looks. #3414. macOS 27.3 adds native Markdown rendering to Quick Look

Starting with macOS 27.3, users can preview Markdown files with proper formatting directly in Quick Look. Here are the details.

Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with new Safari features, including Vertical Tabs and Adaptive Dark Mode, expanded Siri AI capabilities, and new tools for third-party developers.

Among the smaller changes coming to the Mac is a welcome improvement to Quick Look. As of macOS 27.3 beta 1, .md files are rendered with proper formatting directly in Quick Look, rather than displaying their raw Markdown syntax.

Apple has been expanding Markdown support across its platforms, including the ability to import and export Markdown files in Notes. Markdown has also become increasingly important with the rise of AI agents, which use .md files to store instructions, context, and other information.

In fact, as Federico Viticci noted today on X, Apple’s new Siri AI app skills feature also uses Markdown-based SKILL.md files, allowing developers to provide instructions that help Siri perform complex tasks within their apps.

What a journey for Markdown, @gruber The new Siri AI developer framework now officially uses skills, with specific Markdown guidance for SKILL .md agent files https://t.co/koi8K541le pic.twitter.com/TF72JJZRXc

For the uninitiated, Markdown is a simple text formatting syntax created by John Gruber in 2004, and has since become widely used for writing documentation, publishing content online (including this very post), and, more recently, providing instructions to AI agents.

Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for web writers. Markdown allows you to write using an easy-to-read, easy-to-write plain text format, then convert it to structurally valid HTML.

In practice, this means you can create headings, bold text, lists, and links using just a few simple characters. And, starting with macOS 27.3, you’ll be able to preview the results directly in Quick Look, without having to open the file in a separate app.

To learn more about Markdown, follow this link.

#3408. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: eight to 10 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.

Kids might be the most brutally honest gift recipients on the planet. They’ll tell you exactly what they want, change their minds three times before December, and have absolutely no problem letting you know when you’ve missed the mark. Throw in the never-ending cycle of viral toys, influencer collaborations, and pop culture obsessions, and suddenly, buying the right gift requires knowing more about internet culture than you ever signed up for.

Fortunately, our product editors are here to make things a little easier. We’ve rounded up the best gifts for kids in 2026, including the toys taking over TikTok, hands-on activities that don’t require another screen, and collectibles inspired by their favorite characters. From KPop Demon Hunters to sensory toys that are surprisingly hard to put down, these picks cover a range of ages, interests, and budgets. No frantic last-minute toy aisle searches required.

Below, find our favorite toys, viral hits, and genuinely cool gifts for every kid on your holiday shopping list.

The KPop Demon Hunters phenomenon has officially made its way into the toy aisle. This 12.75-inch Rumi doll features five posable joints, her recognizable stage outfit, and a singing function that plays “Golden.”

For the kid who’s already built every Star Wars LEGO set imaginable, this one brings something new to the table. The SMART Play TIE Fighter combines traditional building with interactive lights, sounds, and character dialogue, giving young Jedi (and Sith) plenty to explore.

Jurassic Park has nothing on this Hot Wheels setup. Kids can race through multiple levels, dodge a chomping T-Rex, and send cars flying through loops, all without a single battery.

It’s never too early to develop good listening habits, and we’re not just talking about following directions. The Toniebox Lite introduces kids to music and storytelling through screen-free audio, with interchangeable figures that make choosing what to play part of the fun.

Part robot, part practical joke, this creepy-crawly centipede is guaranteed to get a reaction. Kids can roll it into a ball, sneak it into position, and use the remote to make it burst open and slither across the floor.

Good news: Your kid wants to be a rock star. Better news: This interactive guitar has a headphone jack, so they can experiment with six music modes, built-in melodies, and their own original compositions without turning the living room into a concert venue.

Before viral toys and TikTok trends, there was Tickle Me Elmo. The ’90s sensation returns with a softer, 18-inch design that bursts into laughter and shakes with excitement whenever little hands find his ticklish spots.

A shark with wheels sounds ridiculous until you see this thing in action. Monster Jam’s remote-controlled Megalodon chomps its jaws, performs wheelies, and spins around before breaking free from its chain in Beast Mode.

Mario might get top billing, but Yoshi has always been a fan favorite. This interactive figure hatches from a wobbling, sound-making egg, then comes to life with lights, movements, and plenty of personality.

First came Labubu, now the Care Bears are making their case for the cutest bag charm on the block. Each blind box contains one of six fuzzy collectibles, from perpetually grumpy Grumpy Bear to cheerful Funshine Bear.

Some of the best gifts encourage kids to get a little curious (and maybe a little dirty). This two-in-one digital microscope and borescope camera lets young explorers examine tiny details, investigate hidden spaces, and turn an ordinary walk into a science expedition.

Vinyl collectors, meet your mini-me. This miniature record player actually spins tiny records and plays 30-second music clips, starting with a rock remix of Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony, with additional mini records from artists like Britney Spears and Elton John sold separately.

If your kid keeps stealing your phone to take pictures, this might be the solution. The Momonova camera lets them snap photos, record videos, and print black-and-white pictures instantly, with four rolls of printing paper included.

It’s a beauty haul, it’s a slime kit, and it’s probably going to be all over your kitchen table. Gui Gui’s Mega Slime Haul includes five scented slimes, charms, beads, and miniature tools for creating personalized squishy concoctions.

Santa might need a little extra room in his sleigh for this one. Bluey’s 28-inch-tall house comes with 36 pieces, interactive sounds, and a chimney that projects stars onto the ceiling, making it a standout gift for the show’s biggest (or shall we say little) fans.

The magic here is surprisingly simple, but that’s part of the appeal. A built-in fan sends eight colorful fairies fluttering around the treehouse, while a miniature Gabby figure and accessories keep the imaginative play going.

A life-size-ish Pikachu that actually moves and makes sounds? That’s the kind of Christmas surprise Pokémon fans dream about, especially when this 20-inch puppet offers more than 100 interactive reactions controlled by the person holding it.

Getting kids to eat their greens might be easier with a little help from everyone’s favorite ogre. Grüns teamed up with Shrek for a limited-edition Berry Far Far Away gummy packed with fruit and vegetable ingredients, fiber, and essential vitamins.

They’ve been asking for an Apple Watch since they learned what one was, but this under-$30 alternative might do the trick. It comes loaded with 26 games, a camera, video recording, and a pedometer, giving kids plenty to explore without the grown-up price tag.

Some kids want a puppy for Christmas. Others would rather hatch a prehistoric shark that bursts out of a bubbling egg, flashes its red eyes, and chomps its jaws. Honestly, we respect the ambition.

#3405. Gavin Newsom Commutes Sentences of All 548 Death Row Inmates in California

Governor Gavin Newsom just commuted the sentences of all 548 prisoners on death row in California in what is one of the largest single-day acts of clemency in U.S. history ... but that doesn't mean they're being freed from prison.

Newsom detailed his decision in an open letter Thursday, writing ... "State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us."

The governor added ... "I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency."

Newsom said that while many Californians believe that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die ... he felt as governor that the state cannot morally kill them.

He continued ... "I will therefore issue the same commutation to every condemned person -- life without the possibility of parole, the most severe punishment I can lawfully impose and the state of California can ethically enforce. These offenders will die in prison but not by our hands."

Former President Joe Biden previously commuted the sentences of roughly 1,500 people in Dec. 2024 ... and Oklahoma voters approved a referendum in Nov. 2019 that released or commuted the sentences for 527 inmates -- with 462 released early.

Newsom's commutations come just months after he's set to depart the governorship after completing his second term, with newly elected Dem Xavier Becerra taking over the reins in Jan. 2027.

California has not executed a prisoner since Jan. 17, 2006 ... when Clarence Ray Allen was given a lethal injection.

#3403. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3401. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3398. California Gov. Gavin Newsom Commutes Hundreds of Death Row Sentences

Just days after Democrats took control of Congress, California Gov. Gavin Newsom has commuted the sentences of 548 prisoners on the state’s death row to life without parole.

“State-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us,” Newsom wrote in an open letter Thursday. “I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”

Since the governor is only allowed by state law to give blanket commutations to offenders with one felony, the California Supreme Court will have to approve the commutations of those with multiple felonies — and there’s likely to be a lot of blowback.

According to the New York Times, opponents like Anne Marie Schubert, a former Sacramento district attorney, are likely to challenge the move and allege that Newsom violated the law, arguing that each case should be considered separately. Schubert, who also leads the victims rights group the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation, told the Times she plans to sue the governor, who is rumored to be mounting a 2028 presidential run.

“These are people that have suffered unimaginable losses and were given some sense of finality through the justice system,” she told the paper of victims’ families. “That is all being reopened and rehashed.”

After taking office in 2019, the governor instituted a moratorium on executions, even though the state hasn’t executed anyone in 20 years. Governor-elect Xavier Becerra, who is also a Democrat, has said he’d maintain this moratorium. Still, the state has the largest death row in the Western hemisphere, so Newsom’s decision reduces the number of people on death row in the country by about a quarter.

“This decision is among the most difficult of my career,” Newsom wrote, “not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims’ families.” Still, he wrote that as some cases have been “languishing” for 40 years, the finality of this move may provide comfort for some families. “I won’t pretend I’ve always opposed the death penalty. I used to think the man who killed my sister deserved execution,” Jess Nichol said in a statement. Her sister, Polly Klaas, was killed in 1993 by Richard Allen Davis, who is on California’s death row. “But over time I’ve realized that whether he’s executed has absolutely nothing to do with my recovery or with real public safety. The system tells survivors that execution matters to our healing. It doesn’t. It’s a distraction from what we actually need.”

The death penalty has been in the news lately due to President Donald Trump‘s propensity for executions. Earlier this year, he announced plans to bring the firing squad back to federal prison. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also announced that the execution of Nidal Hasan, the Fort Hood shooter, would be livestreamed in December, before opposition caused Trump to quickly walk back that idea. “The silence after the very breath of a human being is violently wrestled out of them during an execution is deafening. I’ve heard it 14 times,” Reverend Jeff Hood, spiritual advisor to death row inmates, tells Rolling Stone. “Today, Governor Newsom has courageously chosen to break that silence. These commutations represent the height of moral leadership. Cruelty laid down. Now, I’m left with one prayer: God, don’t let any of the governors in the other executing states get any sleep until they find the ethical stamina to follow Newsom’s lead.”

The news comes the same day that three executions are planned in the United States, in Indiana, Florida, and Alabama. It’s the second time there have been three executions in one day in 2026. Florida has been on an execution spree since 2025, with Governor Ron DeSantis signing death warrants for 38 people to date. Critics told Rolling Stone that move is likely politically driven, with DeSantis eyeing the White House; President Donald Trump is a massive supporter of the death penalty. With the next presidential election on the horizon, it seems that the practice could be up for debate on a national level.

The box office is headed to its best year both stateside and global since pre-Covid 2019, with a respective projected $10 billion and near $36 billion.

Despite the recent merger of Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery, Ziffren seemed hopeful that the future of moviegoing wasn’t bound to dim. “Hoping that it’s a successful merger and that it’s not one as others,” said Ziffren.

RELATED: The 65 Movies That Have Made More Than $1 Billion At The Global Box Office

Putting Skydance’s $111 billion Para and WBD merger in context with the massive SpaceX IPO and looming stock market moves by Anthropic and OpenAI, the Ziffren Brittenham LLP co-founder summarized M&A activity as a mixed economic bag.

The YouTube and ESPN deal, with the NFL Network purchase, got some special attention as did the recent revival of the big-bucks Sunday Ticket class action. “Where that’s going to go is anyone guess,” Ziffren said of the case, pondering if the NFL would move to take the matter to the Supreme Court. The attorney also noted that the Sunday Ticket plaintiffs can file a new case now that the bundle is off DirecTV and on YouTube.

RELATED: Bob Iger’s New Magic Kingdom: Fans & Media Wonder If He Can Bring That Disney Sparkle To The Lakers

The NBA — or, more specifically, the L.A. Lakers — received some legal attention from Ziffren with the messy situation of the Buss family civil war that has broken out over their stake in the team with Bob Iger and Josh Kushner’s $12.5 billion purchase in August. A court hearing is set for the Bass sibling squabble on November 15, 2026 in downtown LA.

Turning to a past fave topic of tax credits, Ziffren offered an overview of the proposed The Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, currently before committees in the Senate and House of Representatives. “This legislation is needed by our industry,” Ziffren exclaimed, noting competition and incentives for production globally from more than 55 countries and other jurisdictions. To hit the bottom line, Ziffren opined that the passage of the bipartisan MPTER Act would lead to a surge in production jobs stateside and “$10 billion” for the industry.

RELATED: Newsom’s November Surprise: Boost CA Film & TV Tax Incentives To $1B ASAP, Says Exiting Governor

Supported by strange bedfellows from Donald Trump to Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) even before this week’s midterms, the legislation would let productions eligible for the credit include film and TV productions where the total cost exceeds $1 million and where 75% of the production is in the U.S. There also are provisions for post-production and visual effects. Excluded are news, live sports, talk shows, daytime dramas, social media content, advertising and corporate videos.

Ziffren hoped the “bipartisan period” of the current lame duck Congress would see the federal tax credit pass before the end of the year.

Still, with a deeper look at the big screen, Ziffren emphasized that for the most part, outside of horror films, whenever studios make films that cost under $70M, they tend to lose money. To him, this underscores the vitality of a tentpole investment mind-set at the motion picture studios.

RELATED: Top 50 Classic Horror Movies: A Photo Gallery

“Wide releases are essential to keep that [moviegoing] attendance stable and growing,” Ziffren said. This despite the fall of wide release movies from a level of roughly 100 pre-Covid to 75 in 2024. That number has increased to 94 this year.

While studios pivoted to a day-and-date release model during Covid, when theaters were closed, Ziffren made a point Thursday to underscore how profitable the downstream business is for studios. “Studios can get a lot of money in licensing,” he said, noting that a pay one window can reap as much as $250 million.

After PVOD, studios are licensing to their sister companies in the ad-supported business in what is another lucrative window. “It’s a profitable business once you get in the TV world,” he explained, specifying how the pay TV (or streaming) business has become one with and without commercials. “The only costs in distribution are remittance taxes and residuals, and now and then profit participations,” Ziffren added.

RELATED: The 30 Highest-Grossing Animated Films Of All Time At The Global Box Office

To that, with a mild swipe at algorhythms, Ziffren noted that for all the worries about the effect artificial intelligence will have on the entertainment industry, execs should pay attention to the bottom line. Advocating for studios and streamers to lean into quality over quantity in their battle for eyeballs with YouTube, TikTok, and META’s Instagram, the lawyer noted that AI already has shown it can cut costs.

AI will “lower the costs of post and pre-production, and ultimately production itself,” he noted, as he also said how that will play put in terms of investment is “anyone’s guess.”

As far as the masses’ reception to AI in entertainment, Ziffren acknowledged that “audiences demand will continue to value premium crafted storytelling.” That’s a consensus that many film tracking firms would agree with Ziffren on: Gen-Z audiences have been turned off by the whole notion of AI. It’s a reason why Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey has been so successful grossing $1.8B, Universal and the filmmaker’s top grossing movie ever. Younger audiences have savored the physical craftsmanship on screen.

Harking back to the state of Tinseltown labor, which was the heart of Ziffen’s 2025 speech, the lawyer stated, “AI was not a major issue as it was in 2023.”

Lionsgate Studios posted fiscal second quarter revenue of $667 million, up 41%, beating Wall Street forecasts.

The standalone public company, which separated from Starz in 2025 and has been the focus of heated takeover speculation, narrowed its net loss for the three months ended in September to $15.5 million from $113.5 million the year earlier.

The stock is up 3.5% in after market trade. It’s been buoyed over the past year by deal talk including a reported offer from Legendary Entertainment. Asked about that on a call with analysts after the numbers, CEO Jon Feltheimer said, “We are not going to respond to M&A speculation, but I will say what I’ve said before: that, in this rapidly consolidating environment, I believe we are very well positioned.” Related Stories News Imax CEO Wades Into 'Cliff Booth' Debate: "Frankly, I Don't Understand" News Nexstar Q3 Revenue Nearly Doubles Due To Political Ad Boom; Execs Talk Tegna Appeal, CW Profit Outlook

“Our strong performance in the quarter reflects all of the pieces of our fiscal 2027 plan coming together,” said Feltheimer. “We had very positive momentum in the quarter as we continued to set in place our film tentpoles for the next three years. Combined with another great library performance and continued encouraging signs in our broader operating environment, we have growing visibility into our continued growth trajectory in fiscals 2028 and 2029.” Watch on Deadline

Trailing 12-month library revenue was $1.04 billion, the studio’s second highest ever.

The Motion Picture segment revenue rose 30% year-over-year to $359 million and profit to $89 million driven by the ongoing contribution of Michael and continued library strength.

The next edition in its star franchise, The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping, bows later this month. Lionsgate announced earlier this week that Sony Pictures has come aboard as our international partner and co-financier on Naruto, the film adaptation of the iconic manga. In all, ten of the studio’s next 15 wide theatrical releases are “repeatable branded properties,” Feltheimer noted on the call, including Resurrection of The Christ Parts 1 & 2, The Housemaid’s Secret and Michael 2.

TV production revenue increased 56% to $309 million, and segment profit increased 73% versus the prior year to $21.6 million amid a significant increase in scripted episodic deliveries, including Power: Origins and the second seasons of The Studio and The Hunting Wives. The company anticipates doubling scripted deliveries in fiscal 2027 relative to fiscal 2026.

Feltheimer noted The Rookie: North spinoff will arrive in January on ABC and will stream on Hulu in the U.S. and Disney+ in most international territories.

Lionsgagte is also quietly leaning into its growing Global Products & Experiences Group. In August, it launch the North American tour of the Dirty Dancing musical with the show heading to Broadway in February. It recently announced the full creative team for the La La Land stage musical and will begin workshopping it early next year for a 2028 opening.

The company also debuted Now You See Me Live at the MGM Grand in Las Vegas last month and will be opening a limited run on Broadway next week. And, earlier this week, it announced the expansion of new franchise, The Housemaid, into a stage play shepherded by Tony Award-winning Life of Pi producer Simon Friend to open in the U.K. next September.

Other projects include the Saw: Genesis multiplayer video game, launching in 2027, and the John Wick AAA game in partnership with developer Saber.

“All told, by the end of fiscal 2028, we expect to have at least 8 stage plays, 4 concert tours, 10 live experiences and 9 interactive video games,” Feltheimer said.

Asked if he thinks the business will become financially significant to the company, he said it’s slow going, but yes. “Ballpark, I think we are looking at a run rate by the end of 2028 of revenue of about $50 million and a contribution of over $30 million, so starting to be meaningful and will continue to grow.”

#3389. How to get access to Sonos AI features, as company aims to avoid another app disaster

When Sonos tried a major app update two years ago, things did not go well. Much-loved features disappeared, older speakers experienced connection problems, and accessibility features were broken. That debacle saw the company’s CEO fired.

The company is taking a much more cautious approach as it moves into the AI era with a Sonos 27voice update, enabling natural-language voice control via Hey Sonos requests …

The whole mess started when Sonos launched the company’s first headphones, the Ace, intended to compete with AirPods Max. The app needed to be updated to support these, and the company decided to use it as an opportunity for a ground-up rebuild, launching a completely new app just ahead of the launch.

Customers responded angrily to the loss of key functionality, compatibility issues with older speakers, and accessibility problems. Sonos initially downplayed the complaints, but CEO Patrick Spence subsequently emailed customers to apologize, and provide a timeline for fixes, subsequently making seven promises. However, customers weren’t impressed, and called for Spence to be fired – later getting their wish.

This time around, Sonos started out with a modest update in the form of the Sonos 27 app, leaving the more substantial changes to a subsequent Sonos 27voice version. This will replace the more limited voice control available today, much like the update from old Siri to Siri AI.

Rather than pushing it out to all customers, Sonos is adopting a very cautious approach. First, you’ll have to request early access to the beta and be approved. Second, the company is testing the feature with a relatively small group of users. Third, it’s seeking detailed feedback from beta testers before a planned launch next year.

The new features work in much the same way as Siri on HomePods.

You can use Sonos 27voice at any time by saying the wake word, “Hey Sonos.” While Sonos is listening, the white status light on your Sonos product will glow brighter and the volume will lower if any audio is playing. A confirmation tone will play after Sonos understands your request.

The company says you can then use natural language for both music-related commands and information searches. The company gives the following music examples:

#3387. This Bose Portable Bluetooth Speaker Is 33% Off Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. It hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers.” And right now, ahead of Black Friday, it’s down to $179 from $269, which price trackers show is the lowest it’s ever been.

Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. It’s compact enough to clip onto a backpack using its built-in nylon strap, and tough enough to handle getting knocked around, and sealed against dust and full water submersion with an IP67 rating. Battery life can last up to 20 hours, depending on the volume, which is sufficient for full-day outings. On the connectivity side, there’s Bluetooth 5.4 with AAC and AptX Adaptive support, as well as the ability to keep two devices paired for smoother switching. What you don’t get is a microphone, an aux port, or any voice assistant support, which is worth considering if you prefer wired options or use speakers for calls.

As for its sound profile, it leans into mid- and high-bass, which gives electronic and pop tracks a lively pulse, though at higher volumes, you may notice some compression (which is common in speakers this size). It also doesn’t reach into true low-bass territory, so anyone who wants thumping sub-bass may not get it here, but the punch it does deliver feels clean for its size, notes this PCMag review. And while you won't get the width and separation of a stereo mix since the SoundLink Plus plays audio in mono, its directivity is good—meaning its sound remains clear from different listening positions, so you don't have to sit directly in front of it to get a good experience.

#3385. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3384. Apple still charging 300% of costs on iPhone storage upgrades, says WSJ

Opting for more RAM or storage when buying Apple devices has always been an expensive business, with the company famously charging huge markups.

Apple said in its most recent earnings report that even after the price increases, its margins are being squeezed by higher component costs. But an analysis suggests that the company is still charging three times its own costs for higher storage tiers on the iPhone 18 Pro …

To be fair to Apple, some of the criticism about the premiums charged on configuring a device with more memory or flash storage hasn’t been comparing, well, apples with apples. The SSDs used in Macs, for example, are very much faster than the lower-spec third-party storage cards people typically cite as evidence for the company’s greed.

why are people defending Apple? They are bending everybody over double to keep their profit margins. They buy a billion memory chips or SSD's at a time so they are getting them much lower in price even if the price has gone up.

All the same, there’s no denying that the iPhone maker has always applied extremely high markups to its own direct costs. With the iPhone 17 Pro, for example, upgrading from 256GB to 1TB cost a buyer $400. A Wall Street Journal analysis cited by Macworld says that Apple’s cost at the time was $42, almost a 1,000% markup.

Apple this week warned that memory costs will reduce its holiday quarter profit margins.

When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarters, both company and product gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs. Parekh added that the pressure on Apple’s margins isn’t expected to ease anytime soon.

However, the WSJ’s number-crunching suggests that we probably don’t need to get out the violins just yet. The paper compared the same upgrade on the iPhone 18 Pro, where Apple has increased the price difference to $600. Although the Cupertino company is paying dramatically more, with an estimated direct cost of $192, that still amounts to customers being charged more than three times the price paid by Apple.

#3382. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3381. Dolly Parton’s Manager Dismisses Lawsuit Against Her Nephew

Dolly Parton’s longtime manager has dropped his lawsuit alleging that the singer’s nephew, Bryan Seaver, posed a threat to her business empire after her death.

In a notice of voluntary dismissal filed Thursday, Danny Nozell and his lawyers said they were abandoning the claims without prejudice, meaning they could bring them again. The filing came shortly before Nozell’s deadline to respond to Seaver’s forceful denials of the allegations, and ahead of a hearing scheduled for Tuesday.

Lawyers for both sides did not immediately respond to Rolling Stone‘s requests for comment on the reason for the dismissal or whether the parties had reached a settlement.

At the hearing, a Nashville judge was expected to consider extending a prior restraining order that barred Seaver from coming within 1,000 feet of Parton’s employees and business partners, entering private property controlled by her posthumous company, She’s Alive LLC, or engaging in disruptive or harassing conduct.

The bitter legal feud spilled into public view in September when Nozell sued Seaver in Nashville Chancery Court, accusing him of waging an “obscene, deliberate, and escalating campaign of threats” intended to create “fear and chaos to extort money for his personal gain.” Nozell, who worked with and managed Parton for about two decades, is the sole manager of She’s Alive, a company that oversees the Dollywood theme park in Tennessee and the SongTeller hotel in Nashville, which houses a museum dedicated to Parton. Seaver, the son of Parton’s sister Cassie, vehemently denies threatening anyone.

The initial complaint, filed Sept. 22, cited a series of provocative messages sent by Seaver, which included statements such as, “I am about to become the hand of retribution for my entire family,” and “I’m not an entertainment person. I’m a killer.” In one message, Seaver allegedly threatened to launch a podcast aimed at damaging Parton’s brand partnerships, ending with the apparent demand: “Or fucking pay me.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Seaver forcefully disputed the allegations in court filings last month. He said his “pay me” remark referred to $251,000 he was owed for security services he had already provided to Parton and reflected his frustration with a bank’s new invoicing requirements. He further acknowledged that some of his private messages were profane, but he argued Nozell had taken them out of context to discredit him. Seaver said he was grieving Parton’s illness and death when he sent them, and he claimed that Nozell had encouraged some of his sentiments and even “hearted” a text in which Seaver said he was an arms dealer and mercenary. “Clearly, he wasn’t frightened or intimidated,” Seaver said of Nozell.

Seaver was the family member who announced Parton’s Aug. 25 death in a prerecorded video posted to her Instagram account that drew millions of reactions. According to court filings, he previously worked for private military contractors and provided security for Parton and her properties through his company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services.

In granting the initial temporary restraining order in September, Judge I’Ashea L. Myles said the messages cited in the complaint appeared to combine threats with demands for payment. In her ruling, she cited one message allegedly sent Aug. 19, about a week before Parton’s death at age 80. “I’m going to destroy the entire brand if you don’t get these [Dollywood business partners] out of our bit,” Seaver allegedly wrote.

In his response, Seaver included more context for the texts. In the same text where he mentioned he would “destroy the entire brand,” he went on to say, “I’ll earn you more money by virtue of their exit. Embarrassment on them at every turn is the answer. Let me keep at them. It costs you nothing. I am your ally. This is long game you need to start doing on them. But the judge said the messages appeared to establish a “repeated course of conduct” in which Seaver allegedly coupled “threats with demands for payment or other action,” while invoking “his claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate.” Trending Stories Appeals Court Says Lawsuit Over ‘The Pitt’ Can Proceed, Cites ‘Numerous’ Similarities to ‘ER’ Nicki Minaj Is Going Down With Trump’s Ship After Nearly Every Candidate She Backed Lost As Nicki Minaj Rallied for Trump's GOP, Her Lawyers Told Court She Still Owes Them $295,000 Bob Dylan Meets With Pope Leo XIV in a Private Audience

Seaver was removed from his security role with Parton’s business interests on Sept. 15, according to a letter filed in the case from attorneys for She’s Alive. The letter, obtained by Rolling Stone, made clear that his termination did not affect his separate status as a beneficiary of Parton’s trust.

“The co-trustees will be in contact with you and the other beneficiaries in the near future regarding your interest as a beneficiary of the Trust,” the letter stated. “All parties hope that this will be a smooth transition, and the trust group looks forward to corresponding with you as one of the beneficiaries.”

UPDATED, with final numbers: NBC News‘ midterm Election Night coverage topped major networks, drawing an average of 6.7 million viewers in primetime Tuesday, according to the final figures from Nielsen.

ABC News drew an average of 5.2 million in primetime, followed by Fox News with 4.32 million, CNN with 4.15 million, MS NOW 3.74 million and CBS with 2.76 million.

Overall, 31.2 million watched primetime coverage across 13 networks, according to Nielsen. That is up 23% from the last midterm, in 2022, when 25.4 million watched. It’s down from Donald Trump’s last midterm, when 36.11 million watched. That was the most for a midterm so far this century,

#3378. 'Ocarina of Time' for Switch 2 Might Already Have a Weird Glitch

Thursday is a big day for Zelda fans. That's when the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time officially launches on Switch 2, marking the first major linear (i.e., non-open-world) 3D Zelda game since the 2016 Twilight Princess remake on Wii U. I, for one, have been waiting for this day for years. I loved the N64 original and the 3DS remake, so to have the chance to play a modern take on the definitive Zelda is so exciting—that is, if it actually runs as it should.

I stumbled upon this interesting post on X from Austin John Plays, a YouTuber with a host of Zelda coverage. According to Austin John Plays, Ocarina of Time already ships with a weird glitch that won't necessarily break your experience, but which may slow it down for a while, and perhaps even confuse players into thinking something is wrong with their game or their console.

As his post explains, if you're playing the physical copy of Ocarina of Time, and it's the first game you've ever played on your Switch 2—maybe you got one of those fancy new Zelda anniversary consoles and want to break it in properly?—you may run into glaring performance issues: The game may freeze, your controller may stop working, and the FPS may drop to single digits.

Luckily, Austin John Plays says the fix is easy: just wait. Eventually, your game will boot back to the title screen. When it does, don't try to play right away. Instead, close the game, restart your Switch 2, then try relaunching Ocarina of Time. Austin John Plays advises you may need to repeat this process two or three times, but after that, you shouldn't continue to run into issues. I wouldn't be surprised if Nintendo releases a patch right away for this glitch if it turns out to be as widespread as this post implies.

However, seeing as the game doesn't come out until tomorrow, there's something you can do to prevent it. Austin John Plays thinks the bug only impacts Switch 2 consoles that haven't run other games before. If you've had your console a while, you're likely set. But if you just bought the 40th anniversary Zelda edition of the Switch 2, you might not have had a chance to run a game on it yet. As such, download a game from the e-shop—even a free demo—just to get the system running. Hopefully, that will be enough to circumvent the glitch, and prevent issues when Ocarina of Time launches tomorrow.
